blocks.html: In reading graphs and data you compared bars by their heights. But a mean from a few measurements is only an estimate. Grow 10 more bean plants and the mean height will come out a little different. Error bars show how much we trust a mean. To read them, you need two ideas that sound alike: the standard deviation and the standard error. You met the first in Standard Deviation.

items: Standard deviation (SD, $s$) describes the data: how spread out the individual measurements are.
Standard error of the mean (SE) describes the mean: how far the sample mean is likely to be from the true mean of the whole population.

blocks.html: $$SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$ A bar of the mean ± 2 SE is roughly a 95% confidence interval. If the ±2 SE bars of two groups do not overlap, the difference between the groups is likely real.

Why divide by $\sqrt{n}$? A single measurement can land far from the true mean. But when you average many, the highs and lows partly cancel. The spread of the means you would get from repeated samples shrinks as the sample grows, in proportion to $1/\sqrt{n}$. So four times as many measurements cut the SE in half. The SD does not shrink, because the plants are no less varied just because you measured more of them.

blocks.name: apbio-se
blocks.cap: Drag the sample size. The red bar (±1 SD) stays about the same width; the green bar (±2 SE) narrows.

blocks.title: Standard error from SD and n
blocks.q: Sixteen bean plants have a mean height of 24.0 cm with a standard deviation of 4.0 cm. Find the SE and the ±2 SE interval.
steps: 2 SE = 2.0 cm.
Interval: 24.0 − 2.0 to 24.0 + 2.0, that is 22.0 cm to 26.0 cm.
blocks.a: SE = 1.0 cm; the interval is about 22.0 to 26.0 cm. We are about 95% confident the true mean lies in it.

blocks.title: Do the bars overlap?
blocks.q: Plants given fertilizer A: mean 30.0 cm, SE 1.2 cm. Plants given fertilizer B: mean 25.0 cm, SE 1.0 cm. Is the difference likely real?
steps: The top of B (27.0) is below the bottom of A (27.6): the bars do not overlap.
blocks.a: The difference is likely real: the plants with fertilizer A grew taller.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: The second example as a graph: the ±2 SE bars do not overlap.

blocks.html: Two mix-ups. First, reading overlapping bars as proof that there is no difference. Overlap only means these data do not show a clear difference; a larger sample, with smaller SE, might. Second, swapping SD and SE. Check which one a graph uses (it should say in the caption), and remember the test: more data shrinks the SE, but not the SD.
The "no overlap" rule of thumb is a quick visual check, not a formal test. Its formal partners are the null hypothesis and tests like chi-square, which come next.

blocks.html: In Hypotheses and Controlled Experiments you wrote a hypothesis as a testable prediction. Statistics adds a careful twist: we do not test our idea directly. We test the boring alternative, that nothing is going on, and ask whether the data make it hard to believe.

items: Null hypothesis ($H_0$): there is no effect or no difference. "The fertilizer does not change plant height." "The offspring fit a 3 : 1 ratio."
Alternative hypothesis ($H_a$): there is an effect or a difference. "The fertilizer changes plant height." "The offspring do not fit 3 : 1."

blocks.html: A test asks: if the null hypothesis were true, how likely would data this extreme be? That chance is the p-value. Biologists usually reject $H_0$ when $p < 0.05$. A test weighs evidence against the null; it never proves either hypothesis.

Why test the null instead of our own idea? Because the null makes an exact prediction we can calculate with: no difference, or exactly a 3 : 1 ratio. "The fertilizer helps" does not say how much, so it predicts no single number. Random chance always makes samples differ a little. The test measures whether the difference we saw is bigger than chance alone would usually make.

head: Result
What you say
What you do not say
rows: Reject the null. The data are evidence of an effect.
Fail to reject the null. The data do not show a clear effect.
The null is true. There is no effect.
blocks.cap: The two outcomes of a test and how to report them.

blocks.title: Writing the hypotheses
blocks.q: A student thinks that brine shrimp eggs hatch better in warmer water. She hatches eggs at 20 °C and at 28 °C. Write the null and alternative hypotheses.
steps: The null says the treatment does nothing: temperature does not change the hatching rate.
The alternative says it does: the hatching rate differs between 20 °C and 28 °C.
Her own idea ("warmer is better") is a kind of alternative, but the null is what gets tested.
blocks.a: $H_0$: hatching rate is the same at 20 °C and 28 °C. $H_a$: hatching rate differs between them.

blocks.title: Reading a p-value
blocks.q: The test gives p = 0.21. What should she conclude?
steps: 0.21 is larger than 0.05.
A difference this big would happen by chance about 21% of the time even if temperature had no effect.
That is too common to rule out chance.
blocks.a: Fail to reject the null. The data do not show that temperature matters. They also do not prove it does not; a bigger experiment might show an effect.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: Data like these give a large p-value: the means differ, but the bars overlap a lot.

blocks.html: Saying "we proved the null" when $p \ge 0.05$, or "we proved our hypothesis" when $p < 0.05$. Science reports evidence, not proof. Even a real effect can hide in a small sample, and about 1 time in 20 a true null will give $p < 0.05$ by chance alone. That is why results are repeated.
The 0.05 cutoff is a convention, not a law of nature. Some fields use stricter levels. What matters on the AP exam is to state it and use it the same way every time.

blocks.html: In Dihybrid Crosses you predicted a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio. Real offspring never match a ratio exactly. Is a small miss just chance, or a sign that the genes do not behave as you assumed? The chi-square ($\chi^2$) goodness-of-fit test answers that, using the null hypothesis that the data fit the expected ratio.

$$\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(o - e)^2}{e}$$ with $o$ the observed count and $e$ the expected count in each category. Degrees of freedom = categories − 1. If $\chi^2$ is larger than the critical value for $p = 0.05$, reject the expected ratio.

head: Degrees of freedom
blocks.cap: Critical values of chi-square at p = 0.05 (from the AP Biology formula sheet).

blocks.html: Each term asks how far a category missed, compared with what we expected there. Squaring makes every miss count as positive. Dividing by $e$ scales the miss: being off by 10 matters a lot when you expected 20, and little when you expected 2,000. Why one less than the number of categories? Once the total is fixed, the last category is decided by the others, so only $k - 1$ categories are free to vary.

blocks.title: Two categories
blocks.q: A cross of two heterozygous pea plants gives 400 offspring: 290 purple and 110 white. Do they fit 3 : 1?
steps: Expected: 3/4 of 400 = 300 purple; 1/4 of 400 = 100 white.
$\chi^2 = 0.33 + 1.00 = 1.33$, with 2 − 1 = 1 degree of freedom.
blocks.a: Fail to reject: the data fit 3 : 1. The difference is small enough to be chance.

blocks.title: A dihybrid cross
blocks.q: A dihybrid cross gives 160 offspring: 78, 36, 34 and 12 in the four phenotype classes. Test the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.
blocks.a: Fail to reject: the data are consistent with independent assortment (9 : 3 : 3 : 1).

blocks.cap: Observed and expected counts for the dihybrid example.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: Where 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 comes from.

blocks.html: Three common slips. Using percentages instead of counts (the test needs counts; 10% of 1,000 is far stronger evidence than 10% of 10). Dividing by the observed count instead of the expected one. And using the number of categories as the degrees of freedom instead of one less. Check: your expected counts must add up to the same total as the observed ones.

blocks.html: You know from Proteins that a protein is a chain of amino acids that folds into a shape, and that the shape does the work. Biologists describe that shape in four levels. Each level is held together by different bonds, and knowing which is which explains what heat, acid or a mutation can do to a protein.

head: Level
What it is
What holds it
rows: The sequence of amino acids, from the N-terminus to the C-terminus
Local coils (α-helices) and folded sheets (β-pleated sheets)
Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups
The overall 3-D fold of one chain
R-group interactions: hydrophobic clustering, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges
Two or more chains fitted together
The same kinds of R-group interactions, between chains
blocks.cap: The four levels of protein structure.

blocks.name: bi-molecule
blocks.cap: Step through the levels: chain, helices and sheets, the folded chain, and chains together.

blocks.html: Secondary structure comes from hydrogen bonds along the backbone, the repeating N–C–C chain every amino acid shares. Tertiary structure comes from the R groups. Quaternary structure exists only in proteins with more than one chain.

Why can the backbone fold the same way in every protein? Because every amino acid has the same backbone atoms. The C=O of one amino acid lines up with the N–H of another four amino acids farther along, and a helix forms; lay two stretches side by side and their backbones bond into a sheet. That works almost regardless of the R groups. The R groups differ, so they decide the unique overall fold: oily ones huddle away from water in the middle, charged ones attract their opposites, and two cysteines can join by a covalent disulfide bridge.

blocks.title: Name the level
blocks.q: Hemoglobin is made of four polypeptide chains: two α chains and two β chains. Each chain contains several α-helices. Which levels of structure does that sentence describe?
steps: "Four chains fitted together" is quaternary structure.
"α-helices" within a chain are secondary structure.
Each chain also has its own sequence (primary) and fold (tertiary), so hemoglobin has all four levels.
blocks.a: Quaternary (four chains) and secondary (α-helices).

blocks.title: Cooking an egg white
blocks.q: Heating denatures the protein in egg white. Which levels of structure are lost, and which stay?
steps: Heat makes atoms jiggle hard enough to break weak bonds: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic clustering.
Those hold the secondary, tertiary and quaternary levels, so the fold falls apart.
Peptide bonds are covalent and need much more energy to break, so the amino acid sequence is unchanged.
blocks.a: Secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure are lost; the primary structure stays.

blocks.html: Thinking secondary structure comes from R-group interactions. It comes from hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms, which is why helices and sheets appear in proteins with very different sequences. A quick check: if a bond involves a side chain (R group), it is tertiary or quaternary; if it is between C=O and N–H of the backbone, it is secondary.

Denaturing a protein does not change its sequence, so some small proteins can refold on their own when conditions return to normal. That result showed that the primary structure holds the information for the final shape.

blocks.html: In Levels of Protein Structure you saw that R groups shape the tertiary fold. All 20 amino acids share the same backbone; they differ only in the R group (side chain). For predicting folds, sort the R groups into four families by how they behave in water.

head: Family
What the R group has
Examples (R group)
rows: Mostly C and H; no charge
alanine –CH₃, valine, leucine, phenylalanine (a benzene ring)
An –OH or an amide (–CONH₂) that can hydrogen-bond
A carboxyl group, –COO⁻ at cell pH
An amino group, –NH₃⁺ at cell pH
blocks.cap: The four families of R groups. A few amino acids (such as glycine, cysteine, tyrosine and histidine) are placed differently by different books.

blocks.html: In a protein dissolved in water, nonpolar R groups cluster inside the fold, away from water, and polar and charged R groups sit on the surface, touching water. A swap that keeps the family usually changes little. A swap that puts a charge where a nonpolar group belongs, or the reverse, can wreck the fold.

Water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other and to anything polar or charged. Nonpolar side chains cannot join in, so water around them is forced into a more ordered cage. Folding so those side chains hide together frees the water. That is the hydrophobic effect, the biggest single force in folding. Charged R groups, by contrast, are surrounded happily by water, and opposite charges inside a fold can pair as ionic bonds.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: The –OH can hydrogen-bond, but it carries no charge.

blocks.cap: Sort the R groups into their families.

blocks.title: A swap inside the fold
blocks.q: A leucine buried in the core of an enzyme is replaced by isoleucine in one mutant and by aspartic acid in another. Which mutant is more likely to lose its shape?
steps: Leucine and isoleucine are both nonpolar, with the same atoms arranged a little differently.
Aspartic acid carries a negative charge.
A charge buried in the oily core is not surrounded by water; the fold must change to let it reach water.
blocks.a: The aspartic acid mutant. Leucine to isoleucine usually changes very little.

blocks.title: A swap on the surface: sickle-cell hemoglobin
blocks.q: In sickle-cell hemoglobin, the sixth amino acid of the β chain changes from glutamic acid to valine. The changed spot is on the surface. Why does that matter?
steps: Glutamic acid is acidic (charged) and sits happily in water on the surface.
Valine is nonpolar.
A nonpolar patch on the surface sticks to nonpolar patches on other hemoglobin molecules, so when oxygen is low they link into long fibers.
blocks.a: One charged R group became a nonpolar one on the surface, making the molecules stick together.

blocks.html: Assuming any change of one amino acid ruins a protein. Many swaps, especially within a family or at positions that do not touch the active site, change little; that is why related species can have slightly different versions of the same working protein. What to check: the family of the old and new R group, and where the position sits (inside, surface, active site).

blocks.html: In The Structure of DNA you paired A with T and G with C. College biology adds one more rule that trips almost everyone: every strand has a direction, and the two strands of a helix run opposite ways.

The numbers come from the sugar. Its carbons are numbered 1′ to 5′ ("one prime" to "five prime"). The base hangs on the 1′ carbon, the phosphate on the 5′ carbon, and the 3′ carbon carries an –OH group. In a strand, the phosphate of each nucleotide bonds to the 3′ carbon of the one before it. So one end of the strand has a free phosphate on a 5′ carbon (the 5′ end), and the other end has a free 3′ –OH (the 3′ end).

blocks.name: bi-dna
blocks.cap: One nucleotide: the phosphate on the 5′ carbon, the base on the 1′ carbon, and the –OH on the 3′ carbon.

blocks.html: The two strands of DNA are antiparallel: one runs 5′ → 3′ and its partner runs 3′ → 5′ beside it. New nucleotides are always added to the 3′ end, so strands grow 5′ → 3′. By convention, a sequence written alone is read 5′ → 3′, left to right.

Why only the 3′ end? The enzymes that build DNA and RNA bond the 3′ –OH of the growing strand to the inner phosphate of an incoming nucleotide triphosphate. Breaking off the other two phosphates releases the energy for that bond. A 5′ end offers no –OH to attach to, so no polymerase can extend it. This one fact explains the lagging strand, primers and much of replication.

blocks.name: bi-dna
blocks.cap: Base pairs and the 5′ and 3′ ends of both strands.

blocks.title: Writing the partner beside the strand
blocks.q: A strand reads 5′-ATGCCA-3′. Write its partner directly underneath.
steps: Pair each base: A→T, T→A, G→C, C→G, C→G, A→T.
That gives TACGGT under the strand, letter for letter.
The partner runs the other way, so its left end is 3′.
blocks.a: 3′-TACGGT-5′

blocks.title: Writing the partner on its own
blocks.q: Write the same partner strand in the standard 5′ → 3′ order.
steps: Start from 3′-TACGGT-5′.
Read it from its 5′ end, which is on the right: T, G, G, C, A, T.
This is called the reverse complement.
blocks.a: 5′-TGGCAT-3′

blocks.html: Writing the complement in the same 5′ → 3′ direction as the original: 5′-TACGGT-3′ for the partner of 5′-ATGCCA-3′. That strand runs the wrong way and would not pair. Check by lining the two up: the 5′ end of one must sit across from the 3′ end of the other.
RNA follows the same rules: it has 5′ and 3′ ends and is built 5′ → 3′. That is why mRNA is written 5′ → 3′, the direction a ribosome reads it.

blocks.html: In why cells are small you saw that a cell trades materials through its surface but needs them through its whole volume. Now we put numbers on it. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells both face this limit; they just meet it in different ways.

For a cube of side $s$: surface area $SA = 6s^2$, volume $V = s^3$, so $$\frac{SA}{V} = \frac{6s^2}{s^3} = \frac{6}{s}.$$ As a cell grows, its SA : V ratio falls. Cells stay small, flatten, stretch out, or fold their membranes to keep enough surface for their volume.

Area grows with the square of size and volume with the cube. Double the side: the surface grows $2^2 = 4$ times, but the volume, which needs food and oxygen and makes waste, grows $2^3 = 8$ times. Each square micrometer of membrane must now serve twice as much cytoplasm. Diffusion also slows over distance, so the middle of a big cell would starve. That is why large organisms are made of many small cells rather than a few giant ones.

blocks.name: apbio-cube
blocks.cap: Slide the side length and watch the ratio fall as the cube grows.

blocks.title: Two cubes
blocks.q: Compare SA : V for cube-shaped cells with sides 2 µm and 4 µm.
blocks.a: The smaller cell has twice the SA : V (3 versus 1.5 per µm), even though its surface is only a quarter as large.

blocks.title: Same volume, different shape
blocks.q: A cube 2 µm on a side and a flat box 1 µm × 1 µm × 8 µm both have a volume of 8 µm³. Which has more surface?
steps: Cube: $SA = 6 \times 4 = 24$ µm².
Box: $SA = 2(1 \times 1) + 4(1 \times 8) = 2 + 32 = 34$ µm².
Ratios: $24/8 = 3$ and $34/8 = 4.25$ per µm.
blocks.a: The long, thin box: same volume, 42% more surface. Flattening or stretching raises SA : V.

blocks.name: apbio-cube
blocks.cap: Doubling the side: surface ×4, volume ×8, ratio ÷2.

blocks.html: Life uses every trick. Red blood cells are flat disks. Nerve cells are long and thin. Cells lining the small intestine carry microvilli, and plant roots grow root hairs. Inside cells, the folded inner membrane of a mitochondrion packs more surface for the enzymes of respiration.

Comparing surface areas alone. The bigger cell always has more surface; the question is how much surface each bit of volume gets. Always divide. A quick check: for cubes the ratio is $6/s$, so a larger $s$ must give a smaller ratio.
The AP formula sheet also gives a sphere ($SA = 4\pi r^2$, $V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, ratio $3/r$), a rectangular solid and a cylinder. The pattern is the same: bigger means a smaller ratio.

blocks.html: In Osmosis and Tonicity you predicted where water goes from solute concentrations. Plants add a twist: a plant cell has a wall, and pressure inside it pushes water back out. Water potential (Ψ, the Greek letter psi) combines both effects into one number. You will need molarity from chemistry.

$$\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p \qquad \Psi_s = -iCRT$$ Water moves from higher water potential to lower water potential. Pure water at normal air pressure has $\Psi = 0$. Solutes make $\Psi_s$ negative; pressure (turgor) makes $\Psi_p$ positive.

items: $i$: the ionization constant, the particles each formula unit makes in water (sucrose 1, NaCl 2, CaCl₂ 3).
$C$: molar concentration (mol/L).
$R = 0.0831$ L·bar/(mol·K), the pressure constant.
$T$: temperature in kelvin (°C + 273).
Water potential is measured in bars (1 bar is about 1 atmosphere).

blocks.html: Why does solute lower the water potential? Water molecules that are busy surrounding solute particles are less free to move. So pure water, with nothing holding it back, has the most free energy, and any solution has less: a negative $\Psi_s$. Water flows "downhill" toward lower Ψ, which means toward more solute, unless pressure pushes back. In a plant cell, water enters until the wall presses hard enough that $\Psi_p$ cancels the difference.

blocks.name: apbio-psi
blocks.cap: Change the solute on each side, and the pressure in the cell. Water always moves toward the lower Ψ.

blocks.title: Solute potential of sucrose
blocks.q: Find the solute potential of a 0.1 M sucrose solution at 22 °C.
steps: Sucrose does not ionize: $i = 1$. $T = 22 + 273 = 295$ K.
blocks.a: $\Psi_s \approx -2.45$ bar. In an open beaker, $\Psi_p = 0$, so $\Psi = -2.45$ bar too.

blocks.title: Which way does water go?
blocks.q: A plant cell has $\Psi_s = -7.0$ bar and $\Psi_p = +3.0$ bar. It sits in 0.2 M NaCl at 22 °C. Does water enter or leave the cell?
steps: Solution: NaCl gives 2 ions, so $i = 2$. $\Psi_s = -(2)(0.2)(0.0831)(295) = -9.81$ bar, and $\Psi_p = 0$.
$-4.0$ is higher than $-9.81$.
blocks.a: Water moves from the cell (−4.0 bar) to the solution (-9.8 bar): the cell loses water.

blocks.html: Two slips. Thinking water moves toward higher water potential: it goes from high to low, like a ball rolling downhill. And dropping the minus sign in $\Psi_s = -iCRT$, which makes a salty solution look like it has more water potential than pure water. Check: any solution must come out with $\Psi_s$ below 0, and more solute must give a more negative number.

In the classic potato lab, cores sit in sucrose solutions of different molarity. Where the line of percent mass change crosses zero, the solution is isotonic with the potato, and the potato's Ψ equals the Ψ of that solution.

blocks.html: In Channels, Carriers and Pumps you met the sodium-potassium pump. Here is what it is for. Every living cell has a small voltage across its membrane, the inside slightly negative compared with the outside. Nerve and muscle cells use that voltage to send signals, and mitochondria use a similar charged gradient to make ATP.

The sodium-potassium pump uses one ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, keeping Na⁺ high outside and K⁺ high inside. Potassium leak channels then let K⁺ drift out. The positive charge it carries away leaves the inside negative: about −70 mV in a resting neuron.

blocks.name: apbio-potential
blocks.cap: Step through how the resting potential builds.

blocks.html: Why does K⁺ stop leaking out? Each K⁺ that leaves makes the inside a little more negative, and the negative inside pulls on the positive K⁺ ions, drawing them back. Two forces act on K⁺: the concentration gradient pushes it out, the electrical gradient pulls it in. The voltage settles where they balance. The membrane is far less leaky to Na⁺, so Na⁺ barely moves at rest, even though both its gradients point inward. The pump's own 3-for-2 imbalance adds only a small part of the voltage; its main job is to keep the gradients from running down.

blocks.title: Counting what the pump moves
blocks.q: A patch of membrane runs its pumps through 200 cycles. How many Na⁺ and K⁺ ions move, how many ATP are used, and what net charge leaves the cell?
steps: Each cycle: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, 1 ATP.
Net charge: 600 positive charges out, 400 in: 200 net positive charges leave.
blocks.a: 600 Na⁺ out, 400 K⁺ in, 200 ATP, and a net 200 positive charges out.

blocks.title: Predicting a change
blocks.q: A drug blocks the sodium-potassium pump. The neuron keeps its leak channels. What happens to the resting potential over time?
steps: Without the pump, nothing rebuilds the Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients.
K⁺ keeps leaking out and some Na⁺ leaks in, so the gradients slowly run down.
As the K⁺ gradient fades, there is less to drive the voltage.
blocks.a: The membrane potential gradually becomes less negative, drifting toward 0 mV, and the neuron loses the ability to fire normally.

blocks.html: Thinking the pump alone makes the negative charge. The pump builds the gradients, but most of the −70 mV comes from K⁺ leaking out through channels. Check with the counting: the pump moves only one net charge per cycle, while the K⁺ channels are open all the time.
A nerve impulse is a brief change in this voltage: Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in, making the inside positive for a moment, before K⁺ channels restore it. You met this in Neurons and Signals.

blocks.html: You have toured the endomembrane system and learned where mitochondria and chloroplasts came from. Step back and ask why a eukaryotic cell is divided into so many membrane-bound rooms. The answer is that different jobs need different conditions, and walls let them happen side by side.

Membranes divide a eukaryotic cell into compartments with their own conditions (pH, ions, enzymes), so reactions that would interfere can run at the same time. Membranes also provide surface where enzymes line up in order, as in the folded inner membrane of a mitochondrion and the thylakoids of a chloroplast.

head: Compartment
Its special conditions
What that allows
rows: Breaks down worn-out parts without digesting the cytoplasm (near pH 7)
mRNA is processed before ribosomes reach it
Inner membrane folded into cristae; an H⁺ gradient
Thylakoid membranes in stacks; stroma around them
Light reactions and the Calvin cycle in separate spaces
Enzymes that fold and tag proteins
Proteins for export are made and shipped apart from the cytoplasm
blocks.cap: Some compartments and what their walls make possible.

blocks.name: bi-cell
blocks.cap: Tap the membrane-bound parts: each is a compartment with its own job.

blocks.html: A membrane is a barrier that most ions and large molecules cannot cross without a transport protein. So a cell can pump H⁺ into a lysosome and keep it there, or concentrate one enzyme in one place. The enzymes of a lysosome work best in acid, so if a lysosome bursts, its enzymes do little harm in the neutral cytoplasm. The wall protects twice: it keeps the enzymes in, and the conditions outside keep any escapees weak.

blocks.title: Why pH matters
blocks.q: A lysosome enzyme has its highest activity at pH 5 and almost none at pH 7. What does that mean for a cell if a few lysosomes leak?
steps: Inside the lysosome (pH about 5) the enzyme works well.
The cytoplasm is near pH 7, where the enzyme hardly works.
Leaked enzymes are mostly inactive.
blocks.a: The cell is protected: the enzymes that escape do little damage in the neutral cytoplasm.

blocks.title: A cell with no organelles
blocks.q: A bacterium has no mitochondria. Where does it run its electron transport chain?
steps: An electron transport chain must sit in a membrane so it can build an H⁺ gradient across it.
The bacterium has one membrane that encloses its cytoplasm: the plasma membrane.
Its chain pumps H⁺ out across that membrane, and ATP synthase there lets H⁺ back in.
blocks.a: In its plasma membrane. Some bacteria, like cyanobacteria, also have folded inner membranes (thylakoids) for photosynthesis.

blocks.name: bi-cell
blocks.cap: A bacterium: no membrane-bound organelles, but its plasma membrane does the work of several.

blocks.html: Saying prokaryotes have no compartments at all. They lack membrane-bound organelles, but they use their plasma membrane, and in some species folded internal membranes, for the same jobs. The difference is in how many separate spaces a cell has, not whether membranes do work.

blocks.html: You know from ATP that cells spend ATP to do work, and from Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions that reactions can release or absorb heat. Biologists need one more idea to say whether a reaction can go at all: free energy, the energy available to do work.

The change in free energy, $\Delta G$, tells whether a reaction can happen on its own. $\Delta G < 0$: exergonic, releases free energy, can proceed by itself. $\Delta G > 0$: endergonic, needs an input of free energy. Cells drive endergonic steps by coupling them to ATP hydrolysis, so the total $\Delta G$ is negative.

Free energy combines heat and order: $$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$ where $\Delta H$ is the change in enthalpy (heat content), $T$ the temperature in kelvin and $\Delta S$ the change in entropy (disorder). Breaking a big molecule into small ones usually gives off heat and increases disorder, so it tends to be exergonic. Building big molecules from small ones tends to be endergonic.

Why can coupling work? Free energy changes add. If making a molecule costs $+3.4$ kcal/mol and splitting ATP releases $7.3$ kcal/mol, an enzyme that joins the two into one process gives a total of $3.4 - 7.3 = -3.9$ kcal/mol. The cell does not "use heat" from ATP. Instead, the enzyme usually moves ATP's phosphate group onto the reactant, making a less stable intermediate that then reacts downhill.

blocks.name: bi-enzyme
blocks.cap: An enzyme lowers the activation energy (the hill), but the start and end levels, and so ΔG, stay the same.

blocks.title: Exergonic or endergonic?
blocks.q: Building sucrose from glucose and fructose has $\Delta G = +5.5$ kcal/mol. Breaking sucrose down has $\Delta G = -5.5$ kcal/mol. Which is exergonic?
steps: A negative $\Delta G$ means free energy is released.
Breaking sucrose down is exergonic; building it is endergonic.
The two values are equal and opposite: running a reaction backward flips the sign.
blocks.a: Breaking sucrose down is exergonic.

blocks.title: Coupling to ATP
blocks.q: Glutamic acid + ammonia → glutamine has $\Delta G = +3.4$ kcal/mol. ATP hydrolysis has $\Delta G = -7.3$ kcal/mol. What is the $\Delta G$ of the coupled process?
steps: Add the two: $+3.4 + (-7.3) = -3.9$ kcal/mol.
The total is negative.
blocks.a: $\Delta G = -3.9$ kcal/mol, so the coupled process can go.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: Free energy changes add: an uphill step plus a bigger downhill step gives a downhill total.

blocks.html: Thinking "spontaneous" means "fast". $\Delta G$ says whether a reaction can go, not how quickly. Glucose and oxygen react with a large negative $\Delta G$, yet a sugar cube sits in the air for years, because the activation energy is high. Enzymes lower the activation energy and change the rate; they never change $\Delta G$.
The value $-7.3$ kcal/mol ($-30.5$ kJ/mol) is for standard conditions. In a living cell, where ATP is kept far more concentrated than ADP, splitting ATP releases even more free energy.

blocks.html: In Temperature, pH and Enzymes you saw how conditions change an enzyme's activity. Now we hold conditions steady and change the amount of substrate. The curve you get is one of the most useful graphs in biology.

blocks.name: bi-enzyme
blocks.cap: Reaction rate against substrate concentration. Try the inhibitor sliders later, in the next topic.

blocks.html: As substrate concentration rises, the rate rises, then levels off at a maximum, $V_{max}$, when every active site is busy (the enzyme is saturated). Past that point, only more enzyme raises the rate: doubling the enzyme doubles $V_{max}$.

An enzyme can only handle a substrate when one is in its active site. At low substrate, most active sites sit empty, so adding substrate fills more of them and the rate climbs almost in proportion. At high substrate, an active site is refilled the instant it lets go of a product. Each enzyme is already working as fast as it can, so extra substrate just waits its turn.

College courses describe the curve with the Michaelis-Menten equation: $$v = \frac{V_{max}[S]}{K_m + [S]}$$ $K_m$ is the substrate concentration that gives half of $V_{max}$. A small $K_m$ means the enzyme reaches half speed at low substrate, a sign that it binds its substrate well.

blocks.title: Reading Vmax and Km from data
blocks.q: An enzyme gives these rates (µmol/min) at substrate concentrations of 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 and 40 mM: 11, 17, 25, 30, 33 and 35. Estimate $V_{max}$ and $K_m$.
steps: From 20 to 40 mM the rate rises only from 33 to 35: the curve is nearly flat, so $V_{max}$ is a little above 35, about 37 µmol/min.
Half of $V_{max}$ is about 18.5.
The rate is 17 at 2 mM and 25 at 5 mM, so half speed comes a little above 2 mM.
blocks.a: $V_{max} \approx 37$ µmol/min and $K_m \approx 2.5$ mM. (The data were made with $V_{max} = 37.5$ and $K_m = 2.5$ mM.)

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: The data of the first example: a curve that rises steeply, then flattens.

blocks.title: Using the equation
blocks.q: An enzyme has $V_{max} = 50$ µmol/min and $K_m = 4$ mM. What is the rate at 12 mM substrate? What if the enzyme concentration is doubled?
steps: Doubling the enzyme doubles $V_{max}$ to 100; $K_m$ (a property of each enzyme molecule) stays 4 mM.
$v = \frac{100 \times 12}{16} = 75$ µmol/min.
blocks.a: 37.5 µmol/min, and 75 µmol/min with twice the enzyme.

blocks.html: Thinking more substrate always speeds the reaction. On the flat part of the curve, the enzyme is saturated and the rate barely changes. Check where you are on the curve: if doubling [S] barely changes the rate, the limit is the amount of enzyme, not substrate.

blocks.html: Cells switch enzymes off as often as on. Drugs and poisons often work the same way. An inhibitor is a molecule that slows an enzyme, and where it binds decides how it behaves on the rate curve.

items: Competitive inhibitor: resembles the substrate and binds the active site. Substrate and inhibitor compete for the same spot.
Noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor: binds elsewhere, at an allosteric site, and changes the enzyme's shape so the active site works poorly.

blocks.html: Enough substrate outcompetes a competitive inhibitor: $V_{max}$ is unchanged, but more substrate is needed to reach it (the apparent $K_m$ rises). A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers $V_{max}$, and no amount of substrate brings it back.

blocks.name: bi-enzyme
blocks.cap: A competitive inhibitor sits in the active site.

blocks.name: bi-enzyme
blocks.cap: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds another site and changes the active site's shape.

blocks.html: Picture a crowd of substrate molecules. With a competitive inhibitor, each empty active site gets whichever molecule bumps into it first. Flood the solution with substrate and the inhibitor almost never wins. With a noncompetitive inhibitor, the inhibited enzymes are out of action whatever the substrate does; they are like workers who went home. The rest still work at full speed, so the curve has the same shape but a lower ceiling.

blocks.title: Reading the curves
blocks.q: Without inhibitor, an enzyme levels off at 40 µmol/min. With inhibitor X, the rate is low at small [S] but reaches nearly 40 at very high [S]. With inhibitor Y, it levels off at 20. Name each type.
steps: X: the ceiling is unchanged; high substrate overcomes it. That is competitive.
Y: the ceiling is halved and stays down. That is noncompetitive.
blocks.a: X is competitive; Y is noncompetitive.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: The first example as curves (Vmax 40, Km 2 mM; X raises the apparent Km to 8 mM; Y halves Vmax).

blocks.title: Feedback inhibition
blocks.q: In a pathway A → B → C → D, product D binds an allosteric site on the enzyme that turns A into B. What happens when D builds up?
steps: D binds the first enzyme and changes its shape.
Less A becomes B, so less C and D are made.
When D is used up, it lets go and the pathway restarts.
blocks.a: The pathway slows itself: feedback inhibition keeps D from piling up and saves resources.

blocks.html: Assuming every inhibitor binds the active site, or that more substrate overcomes any inhibitor. Only competitive inhibition can be overcome by substrate. Test it on a graph: if the curve with inhibitor reaches the same top, it is competitive; if its top is lower, it is noncompetitive.

blocks.html: In Photosynthesis the light reactions were a box: light and water in, oxygen, ATP and NADPH out. Now we open the box. It is a small electrical circuit built into the thylakoid membrane, powered by light, and it uses the same trick as mitochondria: an H⁺ gradient that runs ATP synthase. Free energy explains why light is needed: water is a poor electron donor, and pulling electrons off it and lifting them to NADPH is steeply uphill.

blocks.name: apbio-chain
blocks.cap: The thylakoid membrane. Switch between the path of electrons and the path of protons (H⁺).

items: Photosystem II absorbs light; its reaction center (P680) passes an excited electron to the chain. It replaces that electron by splitting water: 2 H₂O → 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ + O₂. That is where the oxygen we breathe comes from.
The electron travels through plastoquinone and the cytochrome complex, which uses the energy to pump H⁺ into the thylakoid space, then through plastocyanin.
Photosystem I (P700) absorbs light again and re-energizes the electron.
Ferredoxin and NADP⁺ reductase hand two electrons to NADP⁺, making NADPH in the stroma.
H⁺ built up in the thylakoid space flows back to the stroma through ATP synthase, which makes ATP (chemiosmosis).

blocks.html: Electrons flow water → photosystem II → electron transport chain → photosystem I → NADP⁺. The products are O₂ (from water), NADPH, and ATP made by H⁺ flowing through ATP synthase.

Why two photosystems? One photon does not carry enough energy to lift an electron all the way from water to NADPH. Photosystem II gives the first boost, the chain spends some of that energy pumping H⁺, and photosystem I gives a second boost. Splitting the climb into two steps lets cells use two photons of visible light per electron.

blocks.title: Counting electrons
blocks.q: A chloroplast releases 3 molecules of O₂. How many electrons came from water, and how many NADPH could they make?
steps: Each O₂ comes from 2 H₂O, which give up 4 electrons.
$3 \times 4 = 12$ electrons.
Each NADPH takes 2 electrons: $12 / 2 = 6$ NADPH.
blocks.a: 12 electrons and 6 NADPH.

blocks.title: Blocking the chain
blocks.q: A chemical blocks the cytochrome complex. What happens to O₂, NADPH and ATP production?
steps: Electrons from photosystem II cannot reach photosystem I, so NADPH stops.
The cytochrome complex no longer pumps H⁺, so the gradient fades and ATP slows.
Photosystem II soon has nowhere to send electrons, so water splitting and O₂ release stop too.
blocks.a: All three fall. The chain is one line; block it and everything after, and soon before, stops.

blocks.html: Thinking photosystem I acts first because of its number. Electrons go from photosystem II to photosystem I. The numbers reflect the order in which they were discovered. A memory check: water is split at the start of the line, and that is photosystem II.
Photosystem I can also send electrons back to the cytochrome complex in a loop (cyclic electron flow). That makes extra ATP but no NADPH and no O₂, and helps balance what the Calvin cycle needs.

blocks.html: The light reactions make ATP and NADPH but no sugar. The Calvin cycle, in the stroma of the chloroplast, spends them to build sugar from CO₂. It is a cycle because the molecule that grabs CO₂ must be rebuilt at the end of each turn.

items: Fixation: the enzyme rubisco attaches CO₂ to a 5-carbon sugar, RuBP. The 6-carbon product splits at once into two 3-carbon molecules of 3-PGA.
Reduction: ATP and NADPH turn each 3-PGA into G3P (glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate), a 3-carbon sugar.
Regeneration: most G3P is rearranged, using more ATP, back into RuBP. The rest leaves the cycle to build glucose, sucrose, starch and more.

blocks.html: Three turns fix 3 CO₂ and make one G3P for the cell, using 9 ATP and 6 NADPH. A glucose (two G3P) takes 6 CO₂, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

head: Step (for 3 CO₂)
Carbon atoms
Uses
blocks.cap: Bookkeeping for three turns of the Calvin cycle. Carbon in equals carbon out.

blocks.name: bi-energy
blocks.cap: The two stages share molecules: ATP and NADPH go to the Calvin cycle; ADP and NADP⁺ come back.

blocks.html: Why does the cycle need both ATP and NADPH? Turning CO₂ into sugar is a reduction: the carbon gains electrons and hydrogen. NADPH supplies them. ATP provides the free energy to make that uphill step go and to rebuild RuBP. Carbon is conserved: the 18 carbons on the table never vanish; only 3 of them, one G3P, are new sugar.

blocks.title: Scaling up
blocks.q: How many CO₂, ATP and NADPH are needed to make 4 G3P for the cell?
steps: Per G3P: 3 CO₂, 9 ATP, 6 NADPH.
For 4 G3P: $4 \times 3 = 12$ CO₂, $4 \times 9 = 36$ ATP, $4 \times 6 = 24$ NADPH.
blocks.a: 12 CO₂, 36 ATP and 24 NADPH.

blocks.title: Turning off the light
blocks.q: Algae in bright light are suddenly put in the dark. What happens in the next few seconds to the levels of 3-PGA and RuBP?
steps: Without light, ATP and NADPH run out.
Rubisco can still fix CO₂ onto the RuBP that is there, making 3-PGA.
But 3-PGA cannot be reduced, and RuBP cannot be rebuilt.
blocks.a: 3-PGA builds up and RuBP falls. This kind of experiment helped Melvin Calvin and his team work out the cycle.

blocks.html: Calling it the "dark reactions" and thinking it runs at night. The Calvin cycle needs the ATP and NADPH that the light reactions make, so it runs in the light, and several of its enzymes are switched on by light. "Light-independent" only means that light does not drive it directly.

blocks.html: Rubisco, the enzyme of the Calvin cycle, has a flaw: it can grab O₂ instead of CO₂. When that happens, the plant loses fixed carbon and energy in a process called photorespiration. You saw in Water Balance in Plants that stomata close when the plant is short of water. Then CO₂ inside the leaf drops, O₂ from the light reactions builds up, and rubisco makes the mistake more often, especially in heat.

C4 plants (corn, sugarcane) separate CO₂ capture and the Calvin cycle in space: mesophyll cells fix CO₂ into a 4-carbon acid, which carries it to bundle-sheath cells where rubisco works in a CO₂-rich spot. CAM plants (cactuses, pineapple) separate them in time: they open stomata and store CO₂ at night, and run the Calvin cycle by day with stomata closed.

head: C3 (most plants: wheat, rice, soybean)
C4 (corn, sugarcane)
CAM (cactuses, pineapple)
rows: Where or when the Calvin cycle runs
blocks.cap: Three ways to run photosynthesis.

blocks.name: bi-plant
blocks.cap: Guard cells close the stomata when water is short. Drag to change the water supply.

blocks.html: The first enzyme in C4 and CAM plants, PEP carboxylase, binds CO₂ even when CO₂ is scarce and does not grab O₂. It works like a pump: it collects CO₂ and stores it in an acid. Later the acid releases CO₂ right where rubisco is, so rubisco is surrounded by CO₂ and rarely makes its mistake. The pump costs extra ATP, which is why C4 and CAM pay off in heat and drought but not in cool, wet places.

blocks.title: Spotting a CAM plant from data
blocks.q: A succulent's leaves are measured at dawn and at dusk. At dawn the leaf sap is very acidic; at dusk it is much less acidic. Its stomata are open at night. What kind of plant is it?
steps: Open stomata at night means CO₂ is taken in at night.
The CO₂ is stored as organic acid, so acid builds up overnight: high at dawn.
By day the acid releases CO₂ for the Calvin cycle, so it falls by dusk.
blocks.a: A CAM plant.

blocks.title: Hot and dry
blocks.q: On a hot, dry afternoon, a wheat plant (C3) and a corn plant (C4) both close their stomata partway. Which loses more carbon to photorespiration?
steps: In wheat, rubisco takes CO₂ straight from the air spaces of the leaf, which is running low on CO₂.
In corn, PEP carboxylase keeps CO₂ concentrated around rubisco in the bundle-sheath cells.
blocks.a: The wheat plant.

blocks.html: Thinking CAM plants run the Calvin cycle at night. At night they only take in CO₂ and store it as acid. The Calvin cycle still needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, so it runs by day, using the stored CO₂ while the stomata stay closed.

blocks.html: In Cellular Respiration glucose and oxygen became CO₂, water and ATP. The first stages take glucose apart and capture its energy, mostly not as ATP but as high-energy electrons loaded onto carriers. Follow the carbon and the electrons, and the stages make sense.

blocks.name: bi-energy
blocks.cap: The four stages of respiration, where they happen, and what they make.

items: Glycolysis (cytoplasm, no O₂ needed): glucose (6 C) → 2 pyruvate (3 C each). It spends 2 ATP and makes 4: a net 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH.
Pyruvate oxidation (mitochondrial matrix): each pyruvate loses one carbon as CO₂ and becomes acetyl-CoA (2 C), making 1 NADH. Per glucose: 2 CO₂, 2 NADH.
Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle, matrix): each acetyl-CoA joins a 4-carbon molecule, and the cycle releases 2 CO₂ per turn. Per turn: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP. The cycle turns twice per glucose.

head: Per glucose
CO₂
ATP
NADH
FADH₂
blocks.cap: All six carbons of glucose leave as CO₂ by the end of the Krebs cycle.

blocks.html: Glycolysis splits glucose into 2 pyruvate (net 2 ATP, 2 NADH). Pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle release all the carbon as CO₂ and load electrons onto NADH and FADH₂. Those carriers, not ATP, are the main product; they power oxidative phosphorylation.

Why does breaking glucose apart give energy at all? The electrons in the C–H bonds of glucose are held loosely. In CO₂, carbon has given up those electrons to oxygen. Each time an enzyme strips electrons and hydrogen off a carbon (an oxidation), it hands them to NAD⁺ or FAD, saving much of the free energy for later. That is why ΔG for burning glucose is so negative, and why cells release it in small steps instead of in one flame.

blocks.title: Tracking carbon
blocks.q: A glucose molecule labeled with radioactive carbon is broken down completely. Where are its six carbons after the Krebs cycle?
steps: Glycolysis keeps all 6 carbons, in 2 pyruvate.
Pyruvate oxidation releases 2 as CO₂.
The Krebs cycle releases the other 4 as CO₂ (2 per turn).
blocks.a: All six are in CO₂: 2 from pyruvate oxidation and 4 from the Krebs cycle.

blocks.title: Counting carriers
blocks.q: A cell breaks down 5 glucose molecules completely. How many NADH and FADH₂ does it make before the electron transport chain?
steps: Per glucose: 2 + 2 + 6 = 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂.
For 5 glucose: $5 \times 10 = 50$ NADH and $5 \times 2 = 10$ FADH₂.
blocks.a: 50 NADH and 10 FADH₂.

blocks.html: Thinking the Krebs cycle makes most of the ATP. It makes only 2 ATP per glucose, the same as glycolysis. Its big product is 6 NADH and 2 FADH₂, whose electrons drive the electron transport chain, where most ATP is made. Check the table: ATP from these stages totals only 4.

blocks.html: The Krebs cycle left us with 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂ per glucose. Oxidative phosphorylation turns their electrons into ATP. It works like the membrane potential of a neuron: a pump builds a gradient of charged particles across a membrane, and the gradient does work as it runs down.

blocks.name: apbio-chain
blocks.cap: The inner mitochondrial membrane. Switch between electrons and protons.

items: Electron transport: NADH gives electrons to complex I; FADH₂ gives them to complex II. They pass through ubiquinone (Q), complex III, cytochrome c and complex IV, losing energy at each step.
Pumping: complexes I, III and IV use that energy to pump H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space.
Oxygen: at complex IV, oxygen takes the spent electrons and H⁺, forming water. It is the final electron acceptor.
Chemiosmosis: H⁺ flows back into the matrix through ATP synthase, which spins and joins ADP and phosphate into ATP.

blocks.html: Electrons go along the chain and end on O₂. Protons (H⁺), not electrons, flow through ATP synthase. Each NADH yields about 2.5 ATP and each FADH₂ about 1.5; with the 4 ATP from earlier stages, a glucose gives about 30 to 32 ATP.

Why does FADH₂ give less ATP? It hands its electrons to complex II, which does not pump H⁺, so they skip the first pumping step. Why is oxygen essential? Without it, complex IV cannot unload electrons; the chain backs up, pumping stops, NADH cannot be recycled to NAD⁺, and the Krebs cycle halts too. Only glycolysis, with fermentation to recycle NAD⁺, can continue.

blocks.title: Estimating the ATP
blocks.q: Use 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂ to estimate the ATP from one glucose.
steps: 10 NADH × 2.5 = 25 ATP.
2 FADH₂ × 1.5 = 3 ATP.
Oxidative phosphorylation: about 28 ATP; plus 2 from glycolysis and 2 from the Krebs cycle: 32.
Moving the NADH made in glycolysis into the mitochondrion can cost some, so books give 30 to 32.
blocks.a: About 30 to 32 ATP per glucose.

blocks.title: A leaky membrane
blocks.q: A chemical makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to H⁺. Electron transport keeps running. What happens to ATP production and to the cell's temperature?
steps: H⁺ leaks back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase.
The gradient is lost, so little ATP is made.
The energy of the gradient is released as heat instead.
blocks.a: ATP production falls and more heat is released. (Brown fat uses a protein that does this on purpose to keep some mammals warm.)

blocks.html: Saying electrons pass through ATP synthase. Electrons travel along the chain and end on oxygen; it is the flow of protons back through ATP synthase that makes ATP. A check: ATP synthase is driven by the H⁺ gradient, and anything that destroys the gradient stops ATP synthesis even while electrons keep flowing.

blocks.html: In Neurons and Signals a neuron passed a message to the next cell with a chemical across a synapse. That is one of several ways cells talk. Every cell in your body is constantly receiving signals, and most of them come from close neighbors, not from far away.

Example

Gap junctions between heart muscle cells; plasmodesmata in plants; immune cells checking each other's surface proteins

blocks.html: Cells signal by direct contact, locally (paracrine and synaptic signals) or over long distances (hormones). Whatever the distance, a signal only acts on a cell that has the right receptor.

Why so many kinds? Distance sets speed and reach. A gap junction links two cells almost instantly, so heart muscle cells contract together. A neurotransmitter crosses a gap of a few tens of nanometers and is cleared in milliseconds, so the message is fast and private. A hormone takes seconds to minutes to circulate but reaches every tissue at once. Cells without the receptor simply ignore it, which is how one hormone can send different messages to different organs.

blocks.name: bi-feedback

steps: A signaling cell releases a signal molecule (a ligand)
The signal reaches a target cell: through a junction, across a short gap, or carried in the blood
The ligand binds a receptor that fits it
The target cell changes what it is doing
opts.title: Every signal, near or far

blocks.cap: The same four steps, at any distance.

blocks.title: Classify the signal
blocks.q: Cells in a healing wound release a protein that makes nearby skin cells divide. Which kind of signaling is this?
steps: The signal is released into the fluid around the cells, not carried by blood.
It acts on nearby cells.
Local signaling by diffusion is paracrine.
blocks.a: Paracrine signaling.

blocks.title: One hormone, different responses
blocks.q: Epinephrine (adrenaline) circulates in the blood. It makes liver cells release glucose and makes heart muscle beat faster, but has no effect on some other cells. Why?
steps: Epinephrine is an endocrine signal: it reaches all tissues.
Only cells with epinephrine receptors respond.
Liver and heart cells have receptors linked to different pathways inside, so their responses differ.
blocks.a: A response depends on the target cell's receptors and on the pathways behind them, not just on the hormone.

blocks.html: Thinking only hormones count as signals. Neighboring cells signal all the time, by contact and by paracrine signals, and a nerve signal crosses each synapse as a local chemical signal. A check: ask how the signal travels. Through the blood: endocrine. Across a short space or a synapse: local. Through a junction or by touching: direct contact.
Bacteria signal too. Many release small molecules and sense how much has built up, which tells them how crowded they are. This quorum sensing lets a whole population switch behaviors at once.

blocks.html: A signal reaches a cell (How Cells Signal). What happens next comes in three stages: reception, transduction and response. The proteins that pass the message along are often enzymes, so switching enzymes on and off is the heart of it.

items: Reception: the signal molecule (ligand) binds a receptor protein. Most ligands are large or polar and cannot cross the membrane, so their receptors sit in the plasma membrane: G protein-coupled receptors, receptor tyrosine kinases, and ligand-gated ion channels. Small nonpolar signals, such as steroid hormones like cortisol, cross the membrane and bind receptors inside the cell.

Transduction: the receptor changes shape and passes the message to relay molecules. Often a phosphorylation cascade: a protein kinase adds a phosphate to the next kinase, switching it on, and so on. Second messengers such as cAMP or Ca²⁺ ions spread the message through the cytoplasm. Phosphatases remove phosphates to switch the relay off.
Response: the last relay changes the cell's activity: it opens a channel, activates an enzyme, or turns genes on or off.

blocks.html: For a surface receptor, the ligand stays outside the cell. The message is carried inside by a chain of shape changes: receptor → relay proteins (kinases, second messengers) → response.

blocks.name: bi-feedback

steps: Epinephrine binds a G protein-coupled receptor on a liver cell
The receptor activates a G protein (GTP replaces GDP)
The G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase, which makes cAMP from ATP
cAMP activates protein kinase A
A cascade of kinases activates glycogen phosphorylase
Glycogen is broken down; the cell releases glucose
opts.title: The epinephrine pathway in a liver cell

blocks.cap: A classic pathway: the hormone never enters the cell.

blocks.html: Why use a relay instead of sending the ligand in? Three gains. The membrane stays sealed, since the message crosses as a change of shape, not as a molecule. Each step is a chance to amplify the signal, because one active enzyme can switch on many of the next. And each step is a point of control, where other signals or drugs can join in, or where a phosphatase or an enzyme that breaks down cAMP can switch the pathway off.

blocks.title: Inside or outside?
blocks.q: Cortisol is a steroid hormone. Insulin is a protein. Where is each one's receptor?
steps: Steroids are small and nonpolar (lipids), so they diffuse through the bilayer.
Cortisol binds a receptor in the cytoplasm; the pair moves to the nucleus and acts as a transcription factor.
Insulin is large and polar, so it cannot cross: its receptor is on the cell surface.
blocks.a: Cortisol: inside the cell. Insulin: in the plasma membrane.

blocks.title: Blocking a step
blocks.q: In the epinephrine pathway, a drug blocks the enzyme that breaks cAMP down. What happens when epinephrine binds?
steps: cAMP is made as usual by adenylyl cyclase.
It is not broken down, so it stays high longer.
Protein kinase A stays active, and the cascade keeps running.
blocks.a: The response is stronger and lasts longer: more glucose is released.

blocks.html: Picturing the signal molecule entering the cell and traveling to the nucleus. For surface receptors, the ligand stays outside; only the message moves in, as a series of shape changes and second messengers. Only small nonpolar signals, such as steroids, actually enter. A check: is the ligand large or polar? Then its receptor is on the surface.

blocks.html: A single hormone molecule can make a liver cell release millions of glucose molecules. The trick is the cascade you met in Reception, Transduction and Response: at each step, one active molecule switches on many of the next.

blocks.name: apbio-cascade
blocks.cap: Change how many each molecule activates and how many steps there are.

blocks.html: Amplification multiplies: if each step activates $g$ of the next, then after $n$ steps one signal gives $g^n$ product molecules. A mutation in a receptor or relay protein can block the whole response, or switch it on for good even with no signal.

Why multiply and not add? Each active molecule in a row acts on its own share of the next row. If one receptor activates 10 G proteins, and each of those leads to 10 molecules of active enzyme, that is 10 groups of 10, or 100. One more step of 10 makes 10 groups of 100: 1,000. Adding (10 + 10 + 10 = 30) would count the molecules of only one branch at each step.

blocks.title: A three-step cascade
blocks.q: A receptor activates 20 G proteins. Each leads to 100 cAMP. Each cAMP (through kinase A) leads to 50 active enzymes. How many active enzymes per signal molecule?
steps: Multiply the gains: $20 \times 100 \times 50$.
blocks.a: 100,000 active enzymes from one signal molecule.

blocks.title: A stuck switch
blocks.q: Ras is a relay protein that passes on growth signals from a receptor tyrosine kinase. A mutation leaves Ras always in its active form. What happens to the cell?
steps: Normally Ras is active only after the receptor binds a growth factor, and then switches itself off.
Stuck "on", it sends the divide signal all the time.
The cell divides even without growth factor.
blocks.a: The cell keeps receiving a signal to divide: uncontrolled division, one of the steps toward cancer.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: A pathway can fail in two ways: always on, or never on.

blocks.html: Adding the gains of the steps instead of multiplying them. If each step activates 10 of the next, three steps give $10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1{,}000$, not $10 + 10 + 10 = 30$. Check by sketching the first two rows: one molecule, then 10, then 10 more under each of those.

Amplification explains two facts about hormones. They work at tiny concentrations in the blood, because the cell multiplies each bound molecule many times over. And responses can be fast, because the cell does not have to make new proteins; it only switches on enzymes that are already there.
Amplification is also why pathways need off switches. Phosphatases remove phosphates from kinases, and an enzyme breaks cAMP down, so the response stops soon after the signal leaves the receptor.

blocks.html: In Blood Sugar: Insulin and Glucagon you saw a feedback loop hold blood sugar steady. Feedback is how cell signals and hormone pathways keep themselves in check. AP questions usually give you data and ask what kind of feedback it shows, or what happens when a loop breaks.

Negative feedback: the response opposes the change, holding a variable near a set point (blood glucose, body temperature, water balance). Positive feedback: the response adds to the change, driving a process to completion (blood clotting, fruit ripening with ethylene).

blocks.name: bi-feedback
blocks.cap: Negative feedback: switch between blood glucose too high and too low.

blocks.name: bi-feedback
blocks.cap: Positive feedback: ripening fruit release ethylene, which ripens more fruit.

blocks.html: A negative loop is self-correcting: the further the value moves from the set point, the harder the response pushes back, so the value wobbles around the set point. A positive loop is self-amplifying: each round makes the next round stronger, so it runs fast until something outside it ends it (the wound is sealed, the fruit are ripe). Living things use positive loops only for changes that should happen quickly and completely.

blocks.title: Reading a graph
blocks.q: After a meal, blood glucose rises from 90 to 140 mg/dL, then falls back to about 90 over two hours while insulin rises and then falls. What kind of feedback?
steps: The change: glucose rose.
The response: insulin rose, and glucose came back down.
The response opposed the change.
blocks.a: Negative feedback. The rising curve of insulin is not positive feedback: what matters is that the response reversed the change in glucose.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: Glucose and insulin after a meal (typical shapes, made-up values).

blocks.title: A broken loop
blocks.q: In a person whose pancreas makes no insulin, what happens to blood glucose after a meal?
steps: The sensor (pancreas cells) can detect high glucose, but no insulin is released.
Body cells and the liver are not signaled to take up glucose.
The loop cannot correct the rise.
blocks.a: Blood glucose rises and stays high: the negative feedback loop is broken.

blocks.html: Feedback works inside cells too. When a cell has plenty of tryptophan, the amino acid itself shuts off the genes that make it (you will see this in the trp operon), and the end product of many pathways inhibits the pathway's first enzyme. Both are negative feedback: more product, less production.

Reading any rising curve as positive feedback. A hormone level may climb steeply in negative feedback too. Ask the right question: does the response oppose the original change (negative) or push it further the same way (positive)? Look at the variable being controlled, not at the hormone.

blocks.html: In Controlling the Cell Cycle you met checkpoints, the places where a cell decides whether to go on. The decisions are made by proteins whose levels and activity change through the cycle, using the same kinase switches as signal pathways.

items: Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) are enzymes that phosphorylate target proteins to push the cell into the next phase. Their amount stays fairly steady.
Cyclins are proteins whose levels rise and fall. A CDK works only when bound to its cyclin. When a cyclin is destroyed, its CDK goes quiet.
One cyclin-CDK pair, called MPF (maturation-promoting factor, also read as M-phase-promoting factor), peaks at the end of G₂ and drives the cell into mitosis; its cyclin is destroyed during mitosis.

blocks.name: bi-chart

opts.xlabel: Time (two cycles; mitosis at the peaks)

blocks.cap: Cyclin rises through interphase and is destroyed in mitosis; the CDK stays level; MPF activity follows cyclin (a sketch of the pattern).

blocks.html: Cyclin levels rise and fall; CDK levels stay steady. A cyclin-CDK complex is active only when enough cyclin is present, and it pushes the cell past a checkpoint. Brakes such as p53 stop the cycle at G₁ when DNA is damaged, allowing repair, or trigger apoptosis (programmed cell death) if the damage is too great.

Why build a switch from two parts? Making and destroying a small protein (cyclin) is a quick, clean way to switch a big enzyme on and off. Destroying cyclin also makes the cycle run one way: the cell cannot slip back into the phase it just left. Checkpoints add safety: a cell copies DNA only if conditions are right (G₁), divides only after copying is complete and correct (G₂), and separates chromosomes only when all are attached to the spindle (M).

blocks.title: Reading the graph
blocks.q: Using the graph, at which point in the cycle is MPF most active, and why does its activity drop suddenly?
steps: MPF activity peaks at the same time as mitotic cyclin, at the end of G₂.
Its CDK is present all the time, so the CDK is not what changes.
During mitosis the cyclin is destroyed, so the CDK has no partner.
blocks.a: At the G₂-to-mitosis transition. It drops when the cyclin is broken down during mitosis.

blocks.title: Losing a brake
blocks.q: A cell has a mutation that destroys its p53 protein. Its DNA is then damaged by radiation. What is likely to happen?
steps: Normally, damaged DNA raises p53, which halts the cycle at G₁ for repair, or triggers apoptosis.
Without p53, the cell does not stop.
It copies and passes on the damaged DNA.
blocks.a: The cell keeps dividing with damaged DNA, so more mutations build up. Loss of p53 is found in many cancers, which are uncontrolled cell division.

blocks.html: Thinking CDKs come and go through the cycle. The CDK is present all the time; it is the cyclin that rises and falls. That is why the enzyme is called cyclin-dependent: its activity, not its amount, follows the cyclin. On a graph, a flat line is the CDK and a sawtooth is the cyclin.

blocks.html: Mendel's law of independent assortment says that alleles of different genes sort into gametes independently. You saw why in How Meiosis Makes Variation: each pair of homologous chromosomes lines up either way in metaphase I. But that only works for genes on different chromosomes. Genes that sit near each other on the same chromosome travel together.

Linked genes are on the same chromosome and tend to be inherited together. In a test cross of a dihybrid, they give mostly parental types (the combinations the parent received) and a few recombinants, made when crossing over swaps segments between homologs.

blocks.name: bi-meiosis
blocks.cap: Step through meiosis. In prophase I, homologs pair and cross over; that is where recombinants come from.

blocks.html: Suppose a fly got the chromosome carrying A and B from one parent and the chromosome carrying a and b from the other. If the genes are on that one chromosome, its gametes carry AB or ab, just as they came in, unless a crossover happens between the two genes in prophase I. Then a chromatid can carry Ab or aB. Crossovers between two close genes are rare, so recombinants are few. If the genes were on different chromosomes, all four gametes would be equally common: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.

blocks.title: Spotting linkage
blocks.q: A fly heterozygous for gray body (G) and long wings (L), which received G and L from one parent, is test-crossed to a black, short-winged fly (gg ll). The 1,000 offspring: gray long 420, black short 410, gray short 85, black long 85. Are the genes linked?
steps: If unlinked, each class would be about 250 (1 : 1 : 1 : 1).
Gray long and black short are the parental combinations: 830 of 1,000.
Gray short and black long are recombinants: 170 of 1,000.
The big excess of parental types means the genes are linked.
blocks.a: Yes, linked. (A chi-square test against 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 would give a huge χ², far above 7.81.)

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: Two tall bars (parental types) and two short ones (recombinants): the mark of linked genes.

blocks.title: Which are the parental types?
blocks.q: A plant got the chromosome with A and b from one parent and the one with a and B from the other. In a test cross, which offspring classes should be most common if the genes are linked?
steps: Parental types match the combinations on the parent's two chromosomes: Ab and aB.
Recombinants are the new combinations: AB and ab.
blocks.a: The Ab and aB phenotype classes. Parental means "as the parent received them", not "dominant-dominant".

blocks.html: Expecting 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 from every dihybrid test cross. That ratio needs genes on different chromosomes (or very far apart on one). When two classes are far more common than the other two, suspect linkage; when you count, the two big classes are the parental types.
You can test linkage formally with chi-square: the null hypothesis is independent assortment (1 : 1 : 1 : 1 in a test cross).

blocks.html: In Linked Genes recombinants were rare. How rare depends on distance: two genes far apart on a chromosome have more room for a crossover between them. In 1913 Alfred Sturtevant, a student in Thomas Hunt Morgan's fruit fly lab, turned that idea into the first genetic map.

$$\text{recombination frequency} = \frac{\text{recombinant offspring}}{\text{total offspring}}$$ A frequency of 1% is one map unit (one centimorgan). Genes farther apart recombine more, so frequencies give the order and spacing of genes. Unlinked genes recombine 50% of the time, the most a test cross can show.

blocks.name: apbio-genemap
blocks.cap: Tap two genes to read the distance between them.

blocks.html: Crossovers happen at places along the chromosome that are, roughly, random. So the chance that one falls between two genes grows with the distance between them, much as the chance that a raindrop lands between two marks on a sidewalk grows with the gap. Why the 50% ceiling? Genes on different chromosomes give 50% recombinants by independent assortment. Genes very far apart on one chromosome usually have one or more crossovers between them, and that also mixes them as if at random: half the gametes end up recombinant, never more.

blocks.title: From counts to map units
blocks.q: In the fly test cross of the last lesson, 170 of 1,000 offspring were recombinant. How far apart are the genes?
steps: Recombination frequency $= 170 / 1{,}000 = 0.17 = 17\%$.
1% = 1 map unit.
blocks.a: 17 map units apart.

blocks.title: Ordering three genes
blocks.q: Recombination frequencies: A–B 8%, B–C 15%, A–C 23%. What is the order of the genes?
steps: The largest distance, A–C (23), must span the other two.
Check: 8 + 15 = 23, so B lies between A and C.
Map: A —8— B —15— C.
blocks.a: A, B, C (or C, B, A: a map can be read from either end).

blocks.title: Placing a fourth gene
blocks.q: A fourth gene, D, shows 5% recombination with B and 13% with A. Where is it on the map A —8— B —15— C?
steps: D is 5 map units from B, so it sits either 8 − 5 = 3 or 8 + 5 = 13 map units from A.
It is 13 from A, so it lies on the C side of B.
Prediction to test: D should be about 15 − 5 = 10 map units from C.
blocks.a: Between B and C: A —8— B —5— D —10— C. Mapping uses many crosses, and each one checks the others.

blocks.html: Two slips. Counting the parental types as recombinants: recombinants are the two small classes in a test cross, the new combinations. And expecting a frequency above 50%: no test cross shows more than 50% recombinants. If your number is above 50%, you probably used the parental classes. For genes far apart, add up short distances (A–B + B–C) to estimate the long one, since double crossovers make long distances come out too small.

blocks.html: In Meiosis, two divisions take a cell with two sets of chromosomes (2n) to four cells with one set (n): meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, and meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Usually the separations are perfect. When they are not, the cells made have the wrong number of chromosomes.

Nondisjunction is a failure of chromosomes to separate. If a homologous pair fails to separate in meiosis I, all four cells are abnormal: two have an extra chromosome ($n + 1$) and two are missing one ($n - 1$). If sister chromatids fail to separate in meiosis II, two cells are abnormal ($n + 1$ and $n - 1$) and two are normal ($n$).

blocks.name: apbio-nondisjunction
blocks.cap: Switch between normal meiosis and nondisjunction in meiosis I or II. One chromosome pair is shown.

blocks.html: Trace one pair. In meiosis I the pair should split, one homolog to each cell. If both go to one cell, that cell has two copies and its sister cell has none, and meiosis II then passes the error to all four products. In meiosis II only the cell where the chromatids stayed together is affected; the other cell from meiosis I divides normally. When an $n + 1$ gamete combines with a normal gamete, the new cell has $2n + 1$ chromosomes (a trisomy); an $n - 1$ gamete gives $2n - 1$ (a monosomy). Such a change in number is called aneuploidy.

blocks.title: Counting chromosomes
blocks.q: A fruit fly has 2n = 8. One pair fails to separate in meiosis I. How many chromosomes are in each of the four cells made?
steps: Normally each cell gets n = 4.
In meiosis I, both homologs of one pair go to the same cell.
Those two cells (after meiosis II) have 4 + 1 = 5; the other two have 4 − 1 = 3.
blocks.a: Two cells with 5 chromosomes and two with 3.

blocks.title: Which division went wrong?
blocks.q: Of four cells from one meiosis in a plant with 2n = 14, two have 7 chromosomes, one has 8 and one has 6. In which division did nondisjunction happen?
steps: n = 7, so two cells are normal.
One is n + 1 and one is n − 1.
Only a meiosis II error leaves two normal cells.
blocks.a: Meiosis II.

blocks.html: Thinking a meiosis II error affects all four cells. A meiosis I error spreads to all four, because both cells of meiosis I are already wrong. A meiosis II error happens in only one of the two cells, so the other cell's two products are normal. Check by drawing the tree: 1 → 2 → 4, and mark where the error is.

Sometimes every chromosome fails to separate, giving gametes with two full sets (2n). In plants, this is one route to polyploidy, which you will meet in speciation: many crop plants, such as wheat, are polyploid.

blocks.html: As you saw in Where Mitochondria and Chloroplasts Came From, these organelles descend from free-living bacteria, and they still carry their own small circular DNA. Their genes follow different rules from nuclear genes, which shows up clearly in pedigrees.

Genes in mitochondria and chloroplasts are not sorted by meiosis. Offspring usually receive these organelles from one parent only: in many animals, including humans, mitochondria come from the mother, and in many plants chloroplasts come through the seed parent. These traits do not show Mendelian ratios.

Meiosis sorts chromosomes in the nucleus. Organelles are in the cytoplasm, and they divide on their own. In animals, the new cell's cytoplasm, and with it the mitochondria, comes almost entirely from the mother's gamete, which is much larger than the father's. So the next generation gets its mitochondria from the mother. No pairs of alleles meet, so there is no dominance and no 3 : 1.

blocks.name: bi-pedigree
blocks.cap: A mitochondrial trait: every child of an affected mother is affected; no child of an affected father is.

blocks.title: Reading the pedigree
blocks.q: In the pedigree above, the affected woman in generation 2 has two affected children. Her affected brother has two unaffected children. What pattern fits?
steps: Both of an affected mother's children are affected.
Neither of an affected father's children is.
Males and females are both affected, so this is not about the X chromosome.
blocks.a: Maternal (mitochondrial) inheritance.

blocks.title: Variegated leaves
blocks.q: A plant has some branches with green leaves and some with white-streaked leaves, caused by faulty chloroplasts. Seeds from flowers on a streaked branch are grown, using pollen from a green branch. What do the seedlings look like?
steps: Chloroplasts reach the seed through the seed parent (here, the flower on the streaked branch).
The pollen supplies no chloroplasts.
So the seedlings get the streaked branch's mix of faulty and normal chloroplasts.
blocks.a: Streaked or pale, like the branch that made the seeds, whatever the pollen source.

blocks.html: Because mitochondrial DNA passes down the maternal line almost unchanged, except for occasional mutations, it is also a useful tool for tracing ancestry and for comparing populations and species, as you will see in Molecular Clocks. A cell holds hundreds of mitochondria, and they need not all be identical, so the severity of a mitochondrial trait can vary among children of the same mother.

Expecting a 3 : 1 ratio, or a pattern of carriers, for a mitochondrial trait. These genes are not paired and not sorted by meiosis. The test is simple: affected mother, affected children (often all); affected father, unaffected children.

blocks.html: In Polygenic Traits and the Environment you saw that height depends on many genes and on food. The environment can do more than nudge a trait up or down: the same genotype can produce strikingly different phenotypes in different conditions.
Phenotype depends on genotype and environment. The same genotype can show different phenotypes in different conditions, while the genes themselves stay the same.

items: Hydrangeas (bigleaf hydrangea): flowers are blue in acidic soil (below about pH 5.5) and pink in neutral to alkaline soil (above about pH 6.5). In acidic soil the plant can take up aluminum, which turns the flower pigment blue.

Himalayan rabbits: the gene for an enzyme that makes dark pigment has an allele whose enzyme works only at cooler temperatures. The ears, nose, feet and tail are cooler than the body, so fur grows dark there and white elsewhere.
Genetically identical plants (cuttings of one parent) grown in sun and shade, or at low and high elevation, can differ greatly in height and leaf shape.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: Cuttings of one hydrangea grown in soils of different pH (illustrative values following the pattern described by university extension services).

blocks.html: Genes code for proteins, but what a protein does depends on its surroundings. An enzyme folds and works only within a range of temperature (Temperature, pH and Enzymes), and a pigment's color can depend on the ions around it. So a phenotype is the result of genes acting in a particular environment. Biologists call the range of phenotypes one genotype can produce its norm of reaction.

blocks.title: Two gardens
blocks.q: Two cuttings of the same bigleaf hydrangea are planted in two gardens. One blooms blue and one pink. Do the plants have different genes for flower color?
steps: Cuttings of one plant have the same genotype.
The difference must come from the environment: soil pH.
The blue one is likely in acidic soil, where aluminum is available.
blocks.a: No. Same genotype; different soil pH gives different phenotypes.

blocks.title: A rabbit in the cold
blocks.q: A Himalayan rabbit is raised somewhere much colder than usual. Predict its fur.
steps: The pigment enzyme works only at cooler temperatures.
In the cold, more of the body surface is cool enough.
Dark fur appears over a larger area than usual.
blocks.a: The dark areas spread farther over its body, though its genes are unchanged.

blocks.html: Thinking that a phenotype that changes with the environment means the genes changed. The genotype is the same; the environment changes how it is expressed. A check: could you move the organism (or a clone of it) back and get the old phenotype? If yes, the change was in expression, not in the DNA.
