blocks.html: In DNA Replication the helix unzipped and each strand served as a template. Now add the rule from The Direction of DNA and RNA: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to a 3′ end. That one rule forces the whole design of the replication fork.

blocks.name: apbio-fork
blocks.cap: Step through a replication fork, enzyme by enzyme.

head: Enzyme or protein
Job
rows: Unwinds the double helix at the fork, breaking hydrogen bonds between bases
Relieves the twisting strain ahead of the fork
Makes a short RNA primer with a free 3′ end
Adds DNA nucleotides to the primer's 3′ end, building 5′ → 3′, and proofreads
Removes RNA primers and replaces them with DNA
Seals the nicks between pieces of new DNA
blocks.cap: The crew at a bacterial replication fork. Eukaryotes use different polymerases for the same jobs.

blocks.html: The leading strand is built continuously toward the fork. The lagging strand is built in short Okazaki fragments, each starting on its own RNA primer and each made 5′ → 3′ away from the fork; ligase joins them.

The two template strands run in opposite directions. On one, building 5′ → 3′ means moving toward the fork, so polymerase simply follows helicase. On the other, 5′ → 3′ points away from the fork. Polymerase cannot build the other way, so it waits until the fork has opened a stretch, then backfills that stretch away from the fork. Each time the fork moves on, a new primer and a new fragment are needed. Every new strand, leading or lagging, is still made 5′ → 3′.

blocks.title: Which strand is lagging?
blocks.q: A fork is moving to the right. The top template strand runs 3′ → 5′ from left to right; the bottom template runs 5′ → 3′. Which new strand is the lagging strand?
steps: A new strand runs antiparallel to its template.
On the top template, the new strand runs 5′ → 3′ left to right, toward the fork: leading.
On the bottom template, the new strand runs 5′ → 3′ right to left, away from the fork: lagging.
blocks.a: The strand built on the bottom template is the lagging strand.

blocks.title: Counting primers
blocks.q: At one fork, the lagging strand is 12,000 nucleotides long, made in Okazaki fragments of about 1,500 nucleotides. About how many primers does the lagging strand need? How many does the leading strand need?
steps: Each Okazaki fragment starts on its own primer.
$12{,}000 / 1{,}500 = 8$ fragments, so about 8 primers.
The leading strand is one continuous piece: one primer at the origin.
blocks.a: About 8 for the lagging strand; 1 for the leading strand.

blocks.html: Thinking the lagging strand is built 3′ → 5′. No polymerase can do that. The lagging strand is built 5′ → 3′ too, in short pieces that point away from the fork. Check any drawing: the arrowhead of every new strand must be at its 3′ end.
Polymerase also proofreads: it can back up one nucleotide and remove a wrong one. With proofreading and later repair, mistakes are rare, but not zero, and those that remain become mutations.

blocks.html: In Transcription RNA polymerase copied a gene into mRNA. Two details matter now. Transcription follows the same direction rule as replication. And in eukaryotes, the first RNA made is not ready to use: it must be processed before it leaves the nucleus.

items: Initiation: RNA polymerase binds a promoter, a DNA sequence just upstream of the gene (in eukaryotes, with the help of transcription factors).

Elongation: it reads the template strand 3′ → 5′ and builds RNA 5′ → 3′, pairing A with U, T with A, G with C and C with G. The RNA has the same sequence as the other DNA strand, the coding strand, with U for T.
Termination: at the end of the gene, the RNA is released.

blocks.name: apbio-splice
blocks.cap: Step from gene to mature mRNA, then switch to the second splice variant.

blocks.html: In eukaryotes, the pre-mRNA gets a 5′ cap and a poly-A tail, and its introns are cut out by spliceosomes while the exons are joined. By keeping different sets of exons, alternative splicing lets one gene make several proteins.

Why process the RNA? The cap and tail protect the mRNA from enzymes that chew RNA from its ends, and they help it leave the nucleus and attract a ribosome. Splicing adds flexibility. Because exons often code for separate parts (domains) of a protein, mixing and matching exons gives related proteins from one gene. That is one reason humans make many more kinds of protein than they have genes. Prokaryotes, with no nucleus, translate their mRNA while it is still being made, and their genes generally have no introns.

blocks.title: From template to RNA
blocks.q: A template strand reads 3′-TACGGATTC-5′. What RNA is made?
steps: Pair each base: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→U, T→A, T→A, C→G.
The RNA runs antiparallel to the template, so its left end is 5′.
blocks.a: 5′-AUGCCUAAG-3′

blocks.title: Splicing a pre-mRNA
blocks.q: A pre-mRNA has exon 1 (120 nucleotides), intron 1 (400), exon 2 (90), intron 2 (650) and exon 3 (150). How long is the coding part of the mature mRNA (not counting cap and tail)? How long if exon 2 is skipped?
steps: Introns are removed; exons are kept.
Skipping exon 2: $120 + 150 = 270$.
blocks.a: 360 nucleotides; 270 with exon 2 skipped. (360 is divisible by 3, enough for 120 codons.)

blocks.html: Two mix-ups. Keeping the introns and dropping the exons: exons are expressed and kept; introns are in the way and removed. And expecting prokaryotes to splice: their genes generally have no introns, and their mRNA is used at once.

blocks.html: You can already read codons with the table (Reading the Genetic Code). Here is how a ribosome does it. It reads a mature mRNA, from RNA processing, 5′ → 3′, three bases at a time, using tRNAs as adapters.

items: tRNA: each carries one amino acid at one end and an anticodon at the other. Enzymes called aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach the right amino acid to each tRNA. The anticodon pairs with the codon, antiparallel.

Initiation: the small ribosomal subunit binds the mRNA and finds the start codon AUG. The initiator tRNA, carrying methionine, pairs with it; the large subunit joins. The initiator tRNA sits in the P site.

Elongation: a tRNA matching the next codon enters the A site. The ribosome joins the growing chain to the new amino acid (a peptide bond). The ribosome shifts one codon; the empty tRNA moves to the E site and leaves.
Termination: a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA) reaches the A site. No tRNA matches it; a release factor binds, the chain is released, and the ribosome comes apart.

blocks.name: apbio-ribosome
blocks.cap: Step codon by codon through the E, P and A sites.

blocks.html: New tRNAs enter the A site; the tRNA holding the growing chain sits in the P site; empty tRNAs leave from the E site. Release factors, not tRNAs, recognize stop codons.

Why three sites? The ribosome must hold the chain steady (P) while testing whether a new tRNA fits (A). Only a tRNA whose anticodon pairs with the codon stays long enough for the bond to form. After the bond forms, the chain hangs on the A-site tRNA, so the ribosome steps along, putting that tRNA in the P site and freeing the A site for the next one. The bond itself is made by RNA in the large subunit, so the ribosome is a ribozyme, an RNA enzyme.

blocks.title: Codons and anticodons
blocks.q: What anticodon pairs with the codon 5′-UUC-3′, and which amino acid does that tRNA carry?
steps: Pair each base: U→A, U→A, C→G. Under the codon, the anticodon reads 3′-AAG-5′.
The tRNA carries the amino acid the codon calls for: UUC is Phe (phenylalanine).
blocks.a: Anticodon 3′-AAG-5′; it carries Phe.

blocks.title: Counting steps
blocks.q: An mRNA reads 5′-GCAUGUUCGGAUAAGC-3′. Which peptide is made, and how many tRNAs enter the A site?
steps: Start at the first AUG: AUG UUC GGA UAA.
AUG = Met, UUC = Phe, GGA = Gly, UAA = stop.
The initiator Met-tRNA starts in the P site; Phe- and Gly-tRNAs enter the A site; the release factor takes the A site at UAA.
blocks.a: Met-Phe-Gly; 2 tRNAs enter the A site.

blocks.html: Putting the growing chain on the A-site tRNA from the start, or thinking a tRNA reads stop codons. The chain rests on the P-site tRNA until the new amino acid arrives in the A site; then it moves over. At a stop codon, no tRNA pairs: a release factor does. Check: the number of tRNAs that enter the A site is the number of amino acids minus one.

blocks.html: In Turning Genes On and Off you saw that cells express only some genes at a time. Bacteria show the logic clearly. Their genes for one job often sit together in an operon: one promoter, one operator (an on-off switch where a repressor can bind), and several genes read as one mRNA. François Jacob and Jacques Monod worked out the lac operon of E. coli in the early 1960s.

blocks.name: apbio-operon
blocks.cap: Switch lactose and glucose on and off and watch the repressor, CAP and RNA polymerase.

items: lac operon (inducible): genes for using lactose. A repressor protein, made by the lacI gene, normally sits on the operator: off. When lactose is present, a form of it called allolactose binds the repressor and changes its shape, so it lets go: on.

Glucose and CAP: when glucose is scarce, cAMP rises and binds a protein called CAP, which helps RNA polymerase bind the lac promoter. So the operon is fully on only when lactose is present and glucose is scarce.

trp operon (repressible): genes for making tryptophan. Its repressor is inactive alone, so the genes are normally on. When tryptophan is plentiful, it binds the repressor (as a corepressor), activating it; the repressor binds the operator: off.

blocks.name: apbio-operon
blocks.cap: The trp operon: on when tryptophan is scarce, off when it is plentiful.

blocks.html: The lac operon is inducible: normally off, switched on by lactose. The trp operon is repressible: normally on, switched off by tryptophan. In both, the small molecule binds the repressor, never the operator.

Each design saves energy in its own situation. Enzymes to digest lactose are a waste unless lactose is around, so their default is off. Tryptophan is needed all the time, so its genes default to on and shut off only when there is plenty, a form of negative feedback. Glucose control adds a priority: glucose is the easier fuel, so bacteria use it first.

blocks.title: Predicting the lac operon
blocks.q: E. coli is grown with lactose and no glucose. Is the lac operon on?
steps: Lactose present: allolactose binds the repressor, which leaves the operator.
Glucose absent: cAMP is high, and cAMP-CAP helps RNA polymerase bind.
blocks.a: Yes, strongly on.

blocks.title: A broken repressor
blocks.q: A mutant makes no working lac repressor. What happens with no lactose (and no glucose)?
steps: With no repressor, nothing blocks the operator.
RNA polymerase can transcribe the genes whether or not lactose is present.
blocks.a: The genes are on all the time (constitutive), even without lactose.

blocks.html: Saying lactose binds the operator, or mixing up the defaults. The inducer (allolactose) and the corepressor (tryptophan) both bind the repressor protein and change its shape. Lac is off by default; trp is on by default. A check: ask what the cell needs when the small molecule is present. Lactose present: make the enzymes. Tryptophan present: stop making it.

blocks.html: Eukaryotes have no operons of the bacterial kind (Operons); each gene usually has its own promoter and its own controls. And their DNA is wound around proteins, so whether a gene can even be reached is part of the control.

items: Transcription factors: proteins that bind DNA. General transcription factors help RNA polymerase bind the promoter. Specific ones bind enhancers, control sequences that can be thousands of bases away; the DNA loops so they touch the promoter. Activators raise transcription; repressors lower it.

Chromatin packing: DNA winds around histone proteins into nucleosomes. Adding acetyl groups to histones loosens the packing, so genes are easier to read: more expression. Adding methyl groups to DNA (on cytosines, often near promoters) usually tightens packing and silences genes.
After transcription: alternative splicing, how long an mRNA lasts, and small RNAs (microRNAs) that block or destroy specific mRNAs all adjust how much protein is made.

blocks.html: Eukaryotic genes are controlled by transcription factors at promoters and enhancers, and by packing: histone acetylation opens chromatin (more expression), DNA methylation usually closes it (less). These epigenetic marks can be copied to daughter cells, but they do not change the DNA sequence.

blocks.name: bi-dna
blocks.cap: The double helix; in the nucleus it is wound around histones, tightly or loosely.

blocks.html: Why do these marks act like switches? Histones are positively charged and DNA is negative, so they cling together. An acetyl group cancels part of a histone's positive charge, the grip loosens, and transcription factors can reach the DNA. Methylated DNA, on the other hand, attracts proteins that pack it tightly. When a cell divides, enzymes copy the methylation pattern onto the new strands, so the daughter cells keep the same genes on and off. That is how a liver cell's daughters stay liver cells.

blocks.title: A drug that blocks deacetylation
blocks.q: A drug blocks the enzymes that remove acetyl groups from histones. What happens to genes that were packed tightly?
steps: Acetyl groups stay on, and more build up.
Chromatin loosens.
Transcription factors and RNA polymerase can reach more genes.
blocks.a: Many of those genes are expressed more.

blocks.title: Deleting an enhancer
blocks.q: An enhancer 5,000 bases upstream of a gene is deleted. The promoter is untouched. What happens to transcription in cells that have the matching activator?
steps: The activator binds the enhancer and, by DNA looping, helps RNA polymerase at the promoter.
With the enhancer gone, the activator has nowhere to bind.
Only a low, basic level of transcription remains.
blocks.a: Transcription falls to a low level.

blocks.html: Thinking epigenetic changes alter the DNA sequence. Acetylation and methylation change how DNA is packed and read, not its bases: ATGC stays ATGC. That is why they can be reversed, and why identical genomes can behave differently.

blocks.html: A muscle cell and a nerve cell in the same body carry the same genome. Yet one is packed with contractile proteins and the other with ion channels. Gene regulation in eukaryotes explains how: each cell type keeps a different set of genes switched on.

Cell types differ because they express different sets of genes, controlled by different combinations of transcription factors. Nearly every cell keeps the whole genome; it is the pattern of expression, held in place by epigenetic marks, that makes a cell specialized.

blocks.name: bi-cell
blocks.cap: Every body cell has a nucleus with the same genes; what differs is which ones are read.

items: Combinatorial control: a gene's enhancers may need several activators at once. With a few dozen transcription factors in different combinations, cells can set up many distinct patterns.
Master regulators: some transcription factors switch on a whole program. MyoD, for example, turns on many muscle genes, including more MyoD.
Evidence the genes are still there: a single cell from a carrot root, grown in a dish, can grow into a whole carrot plant. Many plants regrow from cuttings of a stem or a leaf.

blocks.html: Why does the pattern last? Specialization is reinforced by feedback: a master regulator often activates its own gene, so once on, it stays on. Epigenetic marks then lock it in and are copied at each division. Signals from neighboring cells, as in cell signaling, decide which program starts in the first place.

blocks.title: Which genes are on?
blocks.q: Gene X needs activators A and B. Gene Y needs A and C. Gene Z needs B and D. A cell makes activators A and B only. Which genes are expressed?
steps: X: needs A and B; both present. On.
Y: needs C; absent. Off.
Z: needs D; absent. Off.
blocks.a: Only gene X.

blocks.title: Same genes, different proteins
blocks.q: A liver cell makes albumin; a skin cell does not. Does the skin cell have the albumin gene?
steps: Nearly all cells keep the full genome.
The skin cell lacks the transcription factors (and open chromatin) needed to read the albumin gene.
blocks.a: Yes. It has the gene but does not express it.

blocks.html: Thinking specialized cells have thrown away the genes they do not use. Nearly all body cells keep the whole genome (mature red blood cells in mammals, which lose their nucleus, are a famous exception). A check: if a plant can regrow from one specialized cell, that cell must still hold every gene.

blocks.html: In Mutations you met mutations as changes in DNA. With the codon table and translation in hand, you can predict exactly what a point mutation does to a protein.

head: Kind
What changes
Example (mRNA)
rows: A base changes but the codon still means the same amino acid
A base change gives a different amino acid
A base change turns a codon into a stop codon
An insertion or deletion of bases (not a multiple of 3) shifts every codon after it
AUG UUC GGA → AUG UCG GA…
blocks.cap: Kinds of point mutations, read from the codon table.

blocks.name: bi-central
blocks.cap: The first nine codons of the β-globin mRNA, and the single change (GAG → GUG) that makes sickle-cell hemoglobin. The first Met is removed later, so the changed amino acid is the sixth of the finished chain.

blocks.html: Read the effect from the codon table: silent (same amino acid), missense (different amino acid), nonsense (early stop) or frameshift (reading frame shifted). What the change does to the organism depends on where it falls in the protein and on the environment.

Why are some mutations harmless? The code is redundant: most amino acids have several codons, often differing only in the third base, so many third-base changes are silent. Missense changes matter most when they hit an active site or swap R-group families (Amino Acid R Groups). Frameshifts and early stops usually wreck the protein. Mutations are also the raw material of variation: without them, natural selection would have nothing new to act on.

blocks.title: Classify the change
blocks.q: An mRNA reads AUG UGG CCA UAA. A mutation changes the G at position 6 to A. What kind of mutation is it?
steps: The second codon UGG becomes UGA.
UGG means Trp; UGA is a stop codon.
The protein ends after Met.
blocks.a: A nonsense mutation.

blocks.title: The environment matters
blocks.q: Sickle-cell hemoglobin comes from one missense change (Glu → Val). Two copies of the allele cause sickle cell disease. Why is the allele more common in regions where malaria is common?
steps: People with one copy of the allele are resistant to malaria.
Where malaria is common, that is a survival advantage, so the allele is passed on more often.
Where malaria is absent, there is no such advantage.
blocks.a: The same allele helps carriers in one environment and not in another: its effect on fitness depends on the environment.

blocks.html: Assuming a mutation has the same effect in every environment. Whether a change helps, harms or does nothing depends on conditions: the sickle-cell allele is the classic case. Also check frameshifts carefully: deleting three bases removes one codon and keeps the frame; deleting one or two shifts everything after it.

blocks.html: In Gel Electrophoresis you saw that DNA moves toward the positive pole and small pieces move farther. To give a band an actual size, run a ladder of known sizes in another lane and compare. The comparison has a twist: the relationship is not a straight line in size.

Distance moved is close to a straight line against the logarithm of fragment size. Plot the ladder as distance against log(size), draw the line, and read the unknown off it. A band halfway between the 1,000 and 500 base-pair bands is about $\sqrt{1{,}000 \times 500} \approx 707$ base pairs, not 750.

blocks.name: apbio-semilog
blocks.cap: A standard curve on a log scale. Slide the unknown band and read its size.

blocks.html: Why a log? The gel is a mesh. A fragment twice as long is held back by a roughly fixed extra amount, not twice as much, so each doubling of size takes off about the same distance. Equal ratios of size give equal steps of distance: 4,000 to 2,000 is the same step as 2,000 to 1,000 and 1,000 to 500. On a log scale, equal ratios are equal steps, so the points line up. (Very large and very small fragments drift off the line, which is why we read only between ladder bands.)

blocks.title: Halfway between two bands
blocks.q: An unknown band sits exactly halfway between the 2,000 and 1,000 base-pair bands of the ladder. About how big is it?
steps: Halfway in distance is halfway in log(size).
blocks.a: About 1,400 base pairs (not 1,500).

blocks.title: Not halfway
blocks.q: The 1,000 bp band moved 30 mm and the 500 bp band 40 mm. An unknown moved 36 mm. Estimate its size.
steps: It is $(36 - 30)/(40 - 30) = 0.6$ of the way from the 1,000 band to the 500 band.
blocks.a: About 660 base pairs.

blocks.name: bi-gel
blocks.cap: A gel with the ladder and the two bands from the examples.

blocks.html: A gel can also check a cut. If a 5,000 base-pair plasmid is cut at two sites, the two fragments must add up to 5,000: bands at 3,800 and 1,200, for example. Linear DNA cut at two sites gives three fragments. Adding the fragment sizes back up is a quick test that you read the bands correctly. Uncut circular plasmids are the exception: they run at odd positions because of their coiled shape, so size them only after cutting.

Interpolating on a straight size scale, as if halfway between 1,000 and 500 were 750. On the log scale it is about 707. A check: your answer for a band between two ladder bands should be a bit closer in value to the smaller one, because the small sizes are spread farther apart on the gel.

blocks.html: In Recombinant DNA a gene was cut and pasted into a plasmid. The next step is getting the plasmid into bacteria and finding the ones that took it up. Then, to be sure what you have, you read the DNA: sequencing. Sizing the pieces on a gel is part of both.

items: Transformation: bacteria take up DNA from their surroundings. In the lab, a calcium chloride treatment and a brief heat shock make E. coli take up plasmids. Only a small fraction of cells do.

Selection: the plasmid carries an antibiotic-resistance gene, such as one for ampicillin resistance. On a plate containing the antibiotic, only cells that took up the plasmid survive and form colonies.
Screening: some plasmids also carry a marker gene that the inserted DNA interrupts, so colonies with and without the insert look different.

head: Plate
Cells
Expected growth
rows: Separate colonies: the transformed cells only
blocks.cap: The four plates of a classic transformation lab.

blocks.html: In transformation, cells take up a plasmid; an antibiotic-resistance gene lets only transformed cells grow on selective plates. Sequencing reads the order of bases; in the chain-termination (Sanger) method, fragments that stop at each base are sorted by size, and the order of sizes gives the sequence.

How does chain-termination sequencing work? Copies of the DNA are made with a few special nucleotides (dideoxynucleotides) that lack the 3′ –OH, so no more nucleotides can be added after one is built in (the 3′ rule again). Each copy stops at a random point, ending in a known base, often marked with a color. Sorted by length, the fragments spell out the new strand base by base from its 5′ end. The template is its complement.

blocks.title: Transformation efficiency
blocks.q: Cells were given 0.1 µg of plasmid in 1.0 mL. A quarter of the mixture (0.25 mL) was spread on an ampicillin plate, and 120 colonies grew. What is the transformation efficiency?
steps: DNA on the plate: $0.1 \times 0.25 = 0.025$ µg.
Efficiency = colonies ÷ µg of DNA spread: $120 / 0.025 = 4{,}800$.
blocks.a: 4,800 transformants per µg of DNA.

blocks.title: Reading a chain-termination result
blocks.q: Fragments ending in each base were sorted by length: 1 nucleotide ends in G, 2 in A, 3 in T, 4 in T, 5 in C, 6 in A. What is the new strand, and what is the template?
steps: Shortest to longest gives the new strand from its 5′ end: G, A, T, T, C, A.
New strand: 5′-GATTCA-3′.
Template (complement, antiparallel): 3′-CTAAGT-5′.
blocks.a: New strand 5′-GATTCA-3′; template 3′-CTAAGT-5′ (5′-TGAATC-3′ written the standard way).

blocks.name: bi-gel
blocks.cap: Checking for an insert: cutting out the inserted piece gives a second band of its size.

blocks.html: Thinking every cell on the plate took up the plasmid. On a plate without antibiotic, plasmid-free cells grow too. On an antibiotic plate, only transformed cells survive: the plate selects them, and each colony grew from one transformed cell. That is why efficiency counts colonies on the selective plate only.

blocks.html: You met the Hardy-Weinberg principle in Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium: in a population that is not evolving, allele and genotype frequencies stay the same from one generation to the next. Here we use it as a tool: from one known number, find all the others, and compare real data with the prediction, as in chi-square.

For a gene with two alleles, with frequencies $p$ (dominant) and $q$ (recessive): $$p + q = 1 \qquad p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$$ $p^2$, $2pq$ and $q^2$ are the frequencies of AA, Aa and aa. Start from what you know: usually $q^2$, the share showing the recessive phenotype. Then $q = \sqrt{q^2}$, $p = 1 - q$, and carriers $= 2pq$.

blocks.name: apbio-hw
blocks.cap: The square of genotype frequencies. Slide q and watch the areas change.

blocks.html: Why squares? If parents pair up at random, each new individual gets one allele from a gamete of each parent, drawn independently from the gene pool. The chance of A then A is $p \times p$; of a then a is $q \times q$; and a heterozygote can arise two ways (A then a, or a then A), so $2pq$. The equilibrium holds only under five conditions: a large population, parents pairing at random, no mutation, no migration (gene flow) and no natural selection. When data break the prediction, at least one of these is failing.

blocks.title: From the recessive phenotype
blocks.q: In a population of moths, 16% are white, the recessive phenotype. Find p, q and the share of heterozygous carriers.
blocks.a: p = 0.6, q = 0.4, and 48% are carriers.

blocks.title: From genotype counts
blocks.q: A sample of 200 plants has 90 AA, 80 Aa and 30 aa. Find p and q, and the genotype counts expected at equilibrium.
steps: Observed 90, 80, 30 against expected 84.5, 91, 24.5: fewer heterozygotes than expected.
blocks.a: p = 0.65, q = 0.35. A chi-square test would tell whether the shortage of heterozygotes is more than chance. (When p is estimated from the same data, statisticians use 1 degree of freedom for three genotypes; follow what a problem tells you.)

blocks.html: Two classic slips. Computing $2pq$ as $2(p + q)$, which is always 2. And treating the dominant phenotype share as $p^2$: the dominant phenotype is AA and Aa, so it equals $p^2 + 2pq = 1 - q^2$. That is why you start from the recessive phenotype: only there do genotype and phenotype match.

blocks.html: Natural selection is one way allele frequencies change. Mutation, drift, gene flow and selection are others, and Hardy-Weinberg assumes a large population for a reason. In a small one, chance alone moves allele frequencies around. That random change is genetic drift.

Drift is a random change in allele frequency from one generation to the next, strongest in small populations. A bottleneck (most of a population dies for reasons unrelated to its genes) or a founder effect (a few individuals start a new population) can change frequencies sharply and cut genetic variation.

blocks.name: apbio-drift
blocks.cap: Eight populations, all starting at p = 0.5, with no selection at all. Switch the population size and run again.

blocks.html: Each generation is a sample of the genes of the last one. Toss a coin 10 times and getting 7 heads is common; toss it 1,000 times and 700 heads almost never happens. In the same way, a small population's allele frequency can jump by chance each generation, and once an allele is lost (p = 0) or fixed (p = 1), drift alone cannot bring variation back; only mutation or gene flow can. Large populations drift too, but so slowly that selection usually dominates.

items: Bottleneck: northern elephant seals were hunted to a very small number in the 1800s. They recovered to a large population, but today they have very little genetic variation.
Founder effect: a few birds blown to a new island carry only some of the mainland's alleles, at frequencies that happen to differ from the mainland's.

blocks.title: A founding group
blocks.q: On the mainland, allele B has frequency 0.5. Ten lizards (20 alleles) raft to an island: 5 are BB, 4 Bb, 1 bb. What is the frequency of B on the island?
steps: B alleles: $2(5) + 4 = 14$ of 20.
blocks.a: 0.7, up from 0.5 by chance alone: a founder effect.

blocks.title: Which population drifts more?
blocks.q: Two populations of the same plant, one of 30 and one of 30,000, start with the same allele frequencies and face no selection. Which is more likely to lose an allele in 50 generations?
steps: Chance changes are larger in small samples.
The population of 30 can lose an allele in a few unlucky generations.
blocks.a: The population of 30.

blocks.html: Thinking drift favors helpful alleles. Drift ignores fitness: it can remove a helpful allele or fix a harmful one, especially when numbers are small. If an allele rises because its carriers survive or reproduce better, that is selection, not drift. A check: would the change happen even if the allele did nothing at all? Then it is drift.

blocks.html: In Evidence: DNA and Proteins you counted differences between species: more differences, more distant relatives. If differences in a gene build up at a roughly steady rate, they can do more than rank relatives. They can estimate when two lineages split. Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling proposed this "molecular clock" in the early 1960s.

If a gene changes at a roughly steady rate, then $$\text{time since the split} = \frac{\text{number of differences}}{\text{rate of differences}}$$ The rate is calibrated with a pair of species whose split is dated by fossils. Estimates carry wide ranges, because rates vary between genes and between lineages.

blocks.name: bi-chart

opts.xlabel: Time since the split, from fossils (millions of years)

blocks.cap: Differences between pairs of species plotted against fossil dates: a rough straight line is what makes a clock (illustrative data).

blocks.html: Why would changes be steady? Many mutations are neutral, changing nothing that matters to survival, and neutral mutations become fixed in a lineage at a rate set by the mutation rate. Since mutations occur at roughly steady rates, neutral differences pile up like ticks of a clock. The clock is rough because some genes are under strong selection (and change slowly), generation times differ, and mutation rates differ between groups.

blocks.title: Calibrate, then estimate
blocks.q: Fossils show that species A and B split 20 million years ago; a gene differs at 40 sites between them. The same gene differs at 30 sites between A and C. When did A and C split?
steps: Rate: 40 differences / 20 million years = 2 differences per million years.
Time: 30 / 2 = 15 million years.
blocks.a: About 15 million years ago (with a wide range of uncertainty).

blocks.title: Two genes, two answers
blocks.q: Using one gene, two lineages split about 12 million years ago; using another, about 18. Is one estimate wrong?
steps: Each gene has its own rate, and each rate was calibrated with uncertain fossil dates.
Selection, generation time and chance all vary.
Scientists combine many genes and several fossil calibrations to narrow the range.
blocks.a: Not necessarily. Both are estimates; the true date is likely in the range they span, and more data would narrow it.

blocks.html: Different clocks suit different questions. A gene that changes slowly, such as one for ribosomal RNA, can still be compared across bacteria, plants and animals that split billions of years ago. A fast-changing stretch of DNA, such as many parts of mitochondrial DNA, is better for splits within the last few million years, because a slow gene would show almost no differences over so short a time.

Treating the clock as exact for every gene. Rates differ between genes (a gene for a vital enzyme changes slowly) and between lineages, so a clock must be calibrated and its estimates carry ranges. When a problem gives you a rate, use it; when you report, say "about".

blocks.html: In Building Cladograms you grouped species by shared derived traits. Now we build trees from tables of data, of traits or of DNA differences, and we pick between possible trees with a rule called parsimony. Molecular clocks can then date the branch points.

From a table of differences, the pair with the fewest differences shares the most recent common ancestor; join them first, then add the next closest. With traits, group by shared derived traits. When several trees are possible, parsimony picks the one that needs the fewest changes. Every tree is a hypothesis.

head: Human
Chimpanzee
Gorilla
Orangutan
blocks.cap: Differences in a stretch of DNA (made-up numbers in proportion to the real pattern).

blocks.name: bi-tree
blocks.cap: The tree the table supports. Tap two tips to light up their most recent common ancestor.

blocks.html: Why trust the fewest changes? Each change of a trait or a base is an event. A tree that needs a change to happen twice, independently, in two branches is possible (it is called convergence), but less likely than one where it happened once in a common ancestor. Parsimony is a way of choosing the simplest explanation of the data. It can be wrong, and other methods weigh how likely each kind of change is, which is why scientists test trees with more data.

blocks.title: Joining from a table
blocks.q: Use the table above to build the tree.
steps: Fewest differences: human and chimpanzee (1). Join them.
Next: gorilla differs from both by 2. Join gorilla to that pair.
Orangutan differs from all by 4: it branched off first.
blocks.a: Orangutan first, then gorilla, then human and chimpanzee as closest relatives.

blocks.title: Counting changes
blocks.q: Four plants: moss (no tubes, no seeds), fern (tubes, no seeds), pine (tubes, seeds), rose (tubes, seeds). Tree 1: (moss, (fern, (pine, rose))). Tree 2: (fern, (moss, (pine, rose))). How many changes does each need, if all started without tubes or seeds?
steps: Tree 1: tubes appear once (before fern), seeds once (before pine and rose): 2 changes.
Tree 2: tubes must appear in fern, and separately in the pine-rose branch (or appear early and be lost in moss): 3 changes.
Parsimony prefers tree 1.
blocks.a: Tree 1 needs 2 changes; tree 2 needs 3. Tree 1 is the more parsimonious hypothesis.

blocks.html: Thinking a tree built from data is final. Trees are hypotheses: new genes, new fossils or better methods can move a branch. Also check how you read a tree: closeness is about the most recent common ancestor, not about which tips sit next to each other on the page, since branches can rotate.

blocks.html: In How New Species Form populations stopped exchanging genes and drifted apart. Zoom out to the fossil record and trees built from data, and patterns appear in the pace of speciation, in bursts of new species, and in extinctions.

items: Gradualism: species change slowly and steadily over long times.

Punctuated equilibrium: long periods of little change (stasis), broken by relatively rapid change, often when a new species branches off. Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould proposed it in 1972, from patterns in fossils. Both patterns occur in the record.

Adaptive radiation: one ancestor gives rise to many species that fill different niches, often after reaching new land (Darwin's finches on the Galápagos, honeycreepers in Hawaii) or after a mass extinction opens niches.

Extinction: most species that ever lived are extinct. A steady background rate is punctuated by five mass extinctions. The largest, at the end of the Permian about 252 million years ago, wiped out most marine species. After the end-Cretaceous extinction about 66 million years ago, which ended the non-bird dinosaurs, mammals radiated into many new forms.

blocks.html: Speciation can be gradual or come in bursts after long stable periods (punctuated equilibrium). Adaptive radiation fills open niches quickly, often after a mass extinction. Extinction is a normal part of life's history, at a background rate and in rare mass events.

Why would change come in bursts? A widespread, well-adapted species can stay stable for a long time: stabilizing selection and gene flow hold it in place. A small population cut off at the edge of the range can change faster (with drift and new selection) and may become a new species in a geologically short time. Opening niches has a similar effect: with no competitors, small variations that let individuals use a new food or habitat pay off quickly.

blocks.title: What does "rapid" mean?
blocks.q: A snail species shows no change in shell shape for 4 million years, then a new form appears over about 40,000 years and stays stable. Is that gradual or punctuated?
steps: 40,000 years is 1% of the 4 million years of stasis.
On that scale, the change is a short burst between long stable periods.
blocks.a: Punctuated equilibrium. "Rapid" means tens of thousands of years, quick only against millions of years.

blocks.title: Reading a diversity curve
blocks.q: Counts of marine animal families in the fossil record fall from about 400 to about 200 over a short interval, then climb to 300 over the next 20 million years. Describe the two events.
steps: A drop of 200 out of 400 is a loss of half the families: a mass extinction.
The climb afterward is a radiation into niches left empty.
blocks.a: A mass extinction (about 50% of families lost), followed by an adaptive radiation.

blocks.html: Thinking punctuated equilibrium means species appear overnight. "Rapid" here means tens of thousands of years, quick only against millions of years of stability. Neither pattern needs anything beyond ordinary mechanisms: mutation, selection, drift and the isolation of populations.

blocks.html: Every tree of life has a root. Endosymbiosis explains where eukaryotic cells came from, and the fossil record shows life changing for billions of years. How the very first cells arose is a different question, and one that science is still working on. Here is what is well established, and what is still open.

Possible chemical traces of life in rocks (debated)

Cyanobacteria present by this time; oxygen begins to build up in the air (the Great Oxidation Event)

blocks.html: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, and fossils of microbial life go back about 3.5 billion years. Experiments show that simple organic molecules, such as amino acids, form under early-Earth conditions. How the first cells arose is still an open question, studied through hypotheses such as an "RNA world".

items: Building blocks form readily. In 1952 Stanley Miller, working with Harold Urey, passed electric sparks through methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapor and found amino acids. Geologists now think the early atmosphere had less of those gases, but similar experiments with other mixtures, and amino acids found in meteorites, show that such molecules can form without life.

RNA can both store information and catalyze reactions. Ribozymes, including the RNA at the heart of the ribosome, are enzymes made of RNA. That makes it plausible that early life used RNA before DNA and proteins: the RNA world hypothesis.
Membranes can form on their own. Lipid-like molecules in water assemble into small bubbles (vesicles) with an inside and an outside, a possible start for cells.

blocks.html: Why does RNA get so much attention? A living system needs information that can be copied and chemistry that copies it. In cells today, DNA holds the information and proteins do the chemistry, and each needs the other: a chicken-and-egg problem. RNA can do a little of both, so a world where RNA did both jobs could have come first. That is a hypothesis with supporting evidence, not a settled account; scientists also study hot springs and deep-sea vents as possible settings.

blocks.title: How long did it take?
blocks.q: About how long after Earth formed do the oldest widely accepted fossils of life appear?
steps: Earth: about 4.5 billion years ago. Fossils: about 3.5 billion years ago.
blocks.a: About 1 billion years, and part of that time Earth was too hot and too heavily bombarded for life to last.

blocks.title: What did Miller show?
blocks.q: Which conclusion does the Miller-Urey experiment support?
steps: It produced amino acids from simple gases and energy.
It did not produce cells, nor anything that copies itself.
blocks.a: Some of life's building blocks can form from nonliving chemistry under early-Earth-like conditions.

blocks.html: Thinking the Miller-Urey experiment made living cells, or that the origin of life is settled. It made amino acids. The steps from molecules to the first self-copying cells are an active field of research with several competing hypotheses. The later history, from microbes 3.5 billion years ago to the life around us, is supported by a deep fossil and genetic record.

blocks.html: In Group Behavior animals worked together. Here we look at how single organisms respond to cues in their surroundings, and at the signals they send each other. The responses are adaptations: they help an organism find food, avoid danger and survive.

head: Response
What it is
Example
rows: Growth toward or away from a stimulus
A response to the length of night
Some plants flower only when nights are long, others only when nights are short
A change in how fast or how often an animal moves or turns, with no set direction
Pill bugs move more in dry places and slow down in damp ones, so they end up gathering where it is damp
Movement directly toward or away from a stimulus
Many moths fly toward light; trout swim to face the current
The honeybee waggle dance; alarm calls; ant scent trails
blocks.cap: Kinds of responses to the environment.

blocks.html: Organisms respond to environmental cues. A taxis has a direction (toward or away from the stimulus). A kinesis is a change in the rate of movement or turning, with no set direction. Communication passes information between individuals: the waggle dance tells other honeybees the direction and distance of food.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: Moths fly straight toward a porch light
Pill bugs wander fast in dry soil and slow down in damp soil
cards.why: No direction is chosen; only the speed changes, and they collect where they slow down.

cards.text: A seedling bends toward a window
cards.why: Plants respond by growing, not by moving from place to place.

cards.text: Fish swim upstream, facing the current

blocks.html: How can a kinesis bring animals to a good spot without any steering? An animal that moves fast in bad places and slowly in good ones spends more time in the good ones, the way cars bunch up where the road slows. A taxis is more direct but needs senses that detect where a stimulus comes from. Communication pays off when sharing information helps relatives or the group: a bee that reports a rich patch of flowers helps its whole colony, which is made of its sisters.

In the waggle dance, studied by Karl von Frisch, a forager returning to the dark hive dances a figure eight on the comb. The angle of the straight "waggle run" from vertical shows the direction of the food relative to the sun, and the length of the waggle run shows the distance.

blocks.title: Taxis or kinesis?
blocks.q: In a dish that is wet on one side, pill bugs placed at random move quickly and turn often on the dry side, and slow down on the wet side. After 10 minutes most are on the wet side. Taxis or kinesis?
steps: The pill bugs do not head straight for the water.
They change how fast and how much they move depending on humidity.
They gather where they move least.
blocks.a: Kinesis.

blocks.title: Testing the result
blocks.q: Of 40 pill bugs, 30 end on the wet side and 10 on the dry side. Is that more than chance? (Expected with no preference: 20 and 20.)
steps: One degree of freedom: the critical value is 3.84.
blocks.a: Reject the null hypothesis of no preference: the pill bugs prefer the wet side. (A chi-square test again.)

blocks.html: Confusing taxis and kinesis. Taxis has a direction (toward light, against the current); kinesis is a change in how much the animal moves, with no set direction. Ask: did the animal aim for the stimulus, or did it just speed up and slow down?

blocks.html: Every organism spends the energy in its food on staying alive, moving, growing and making offspring. How the budget is split depends on how the animal controls its temperature, and on its size, which brings back surface area to volume. Energy flow through an ecosystem is the sum of all these budgets.

items: Endotherms (birds and mammals) keep a warm, steady body temperature using heat from their own metabolism. That costs a lot: they need far more food than an ectotherm of the same size.
Ectotherms (most fish, amphibians, reptiles and invertebrates) take their body heat mostly from the environment. They need less food, but they are slower in the cold.
Per gram, small endotherms burn energy much faster than large ones: a shrew or a mouse has a far higher metabolic rate per gram than an elephant.

blocks.html: Endotherms spend much of their energy keeping warm, so they need more food per gram than ectotherms. The smaller an endotherm, the higher its metabolic rate per gram. What is left of an animal's intake after metabolism goes to growth, storage and offspring.

series.name: Resting metabolic rate per gram (relative to the elephant)

blocks.cap: Smaller mammals burn energy faster per gram (rounded, illustrative ratios following the well-known pattern).

blocks.html: Why should a small endotherm burn more per gram? Heat is made in the whole volume of the body but lost through the surface. A small body has a high SA : V ratio, so it loses heat quickly for its size and must make heat quickly to keep up. A large animal has relatively little surface and holds its heat. Ectotherms do not pay this cost, which is why a lizard can live on a small fraction of the food a mouse of the same mass needs.

blocks.title: A caterpillar's budget
blocks.q: A caterpillar eats leaves containing 300 J. It passes 150 J as feces and uses 100 J in cellular respiration. How much energy goes into growth?
steps: Energy absorbed: $300 - 150 = 150$ J.
Left after respiration: $150 - 100 = 50$ J.
Only 50 of the 300 J becomes new caterpillar tissue: food for the next level of the food chain.
blocks.a: 50 J (one sixth of what it ate).

blocks.title: Who needs more food?
blocks.q: A 30-gram mouse and a 30-gram lizard live in the same desert. Which needs more food per day, and why?
steps: The mouse is an endotherm; the lizard an ectotherm.
The mouse must make its own heat all day and night.
The lizard warms itself in the sun and lets its body cool at night.
blocks.a: The mouse, by a wide margin: most of its energy goes to keeping warm.

blocks.html: Thinking bigger animals burn more energy per gram. An elephant uses more energy in total than a shrew, but far less per gram. Always check whether a question asks about the whole animal or per unit of mass.

blocks.html: Producers capture the energy that runs nearly every ecosystem. How much they capture, and how much they keep, are measured as productivity. The idea connects energy budgets with respiration: producers spend part of what they make on their own respiration.

Gross primary productivity (GPP) is all the energy producers capture by photosynthesis. Net primary productivity (NPP) is what is left after their own respiration (R): $$NPP = GPP - R$$ NPP is the energy available to the rest of the ecosystem, and it shows up as new plant or algal biomass.

blocks.name: apbio-bottles
blocks.cap: The light and dark bottle method, worked through.

blocks.html: How do bottles separate the two? Fill bottles with pond water and measure dissolved oxygen. In a clear bottle in the light, algae photosynthesize (adding O₂) and respire (using O₂) at once, so the change shows the net. In a dark bottle, photosynthesis stops but respiration goes on, so the drop in O₂ shows respiration alone. Add respiration back to the net and you get the gross. Oxygen stands in for energy because photosynthesis releases one O₂ for each CO₂ fixed.

blocks.title: Light and dark bottles
blocks.q: Pond water starts at 8.0 mg O₂/L. After 24 hours, a light bottle reads 9.5 and a dark bottle 7.0. Find NPP, R and GPP.
steps: NPP = light − start = 9.5 − 8.0 = 1.5 mg O₂/L per day.
R = start − dark = 8.0 − 7.0 = 1.0 mg O₂/L per day.
GPP = NPP + R = 1.5 + 1.0 = 2.5, which is also light − dark = 9.5 − 7.0.
blocks.a: NPP = 1.5, R = 1.0, GPP = 2.5 mg O₂/L per day.

blocks.title: Rates per hour
blocks.q: In a 6-hour experiment, a light bottle gains 1.8 mg O₂/L and a dark bottle loses 0.6. What is the gross productivity per hour?
steps: GPP over 6 hours = 1.8 + 0.6 = 2.4 mg O₂/L.
Per hour: 2.4 / 6 = 0.4 mg O₂/L.
blocks.a: 0.4 mg O₂/L per hour.

blocks.html: Across Earth, NPP per square meter is highest in tropical rainforests, coral reefs and estuaries, and lowest in deserts and the open ocean. But the open ocean is so vast that it contributes a large share of Earth's total NPP, mostly from microscopic algae.

Two slips: subtracting in the wrong direction (respiration is start − dark, a loss), and thinking the light bottle measures gross productivity. The light bottle shows net, because the algae in it respire too. Add the dark bottle's respiration to get gross. Check: GPP must be the largest of the three numbers.

blocks.html: In Exponential and Logistic Growth you saw the J-curve and the S-curve. Now we use their equations to calculate how fast a population is growing at a given size.

Change in population: $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = B - D$ (births minus deaths per unit time). Exponential growth: $$\frac{dN}{dt} = rN$$ Logistic growth: $$\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\,\frac{K - N}{K}$$ $r$ is the per-capita growth rate and $K$ the carrying capacity. Logistic growth slows as $N$ nears $K$ and is fastest at $N = K/2$.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: The S-curve. The dashed line marks K/2, where growth is fastest. Change r and K.

blocks.html: The factor $(K - N)/K$ is the share of the carrying capacity still unused. When $N$ is small, it is close to 1, so growth is almost exponential. When $N = K$, it is 0, so growth stops: births balance deaths. In between, growth is the product of two things pulling in opposite directions: more individuals to have offspring ($N$) and less room left ($K - N$). Their product $N(K - N)$ is largest halfway, at $N = K/2$.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: Logistic growth rate against N: an upside-down U with its top at K/2.

blocks.title: Exponential growth
blocks.q: A population of 400 rabbits has r = 0.3 per year with no limits. How fast is it growing?
steps: $dN/dt = rN = 0.3 \times 400 = 120$ rabbits per year.
blocks.a: 120 rabbits per year (and faster as it grows).

blocks.title: Logistic growth
blocks.q: The same rabbits live where K = 1,000. Find the growth rate at N = 400 and at N = 900.
steps: N = 900: $0.3 \times 900 \times \frac{100}{1000} = 270 \times 0.1 = 27$ per year.
Fastest at N = 500: $0.3 \times 500 \times 0.5 = 75$ per year.
blocks.a: 72 rabbits per year at N = 400 and 27 at N = 900.

blocks.html: Where does $r$ come from? It is the per-capita rate: births minus deaths, divided by the population size. A herd of 1,000 deer with 300 births and 100 deaths in a year has $r = (300 - 100)/1{,}000 = 0.2$ per year, and it grows by $dN/dt = 200$ deer per year. In the logistic model, what slows growth near $K$ are density-dependent factors you met before: competition for food and space, disease and predators all bite harder in a crowded population, raising deaths or lowering births until they balance.

Plugging in N = K and expecting the fastest growth. At $N = K$ the factor $(K - N)/K$ is zero, so growth is zero. Growth is fastest at $N = K/2$. Check: the logistic rate can never exceed the exponential rate $rN$ at the same $N$. And if $N$ is above $K$, for example after a good year, the formula gives a negative rate: the population shrinks back toward $K$.

blocks.html: In Biodiversity and Human Impact you saw why diversity matters. To compare two places, ecologists need a number. Counting species (richness) is a start, but a meadow with 10 species where one makes up 95% of the plants is less diverse than one where all 10 are common. Simpson's diversity index captures both.

$$D = 1 - \sum \left(\frac{n}{N}\right)^2$$ $n$ is the number of individuals of each species and $N$ the total. $D$ runs from 0 (only one species) toward 1 (many species, evenly spread). It rewards both richness (more species) and evenness (similar numbers of each).

Each fraction $n/N$ is the chance that one randomly picked individual belongs to that species, so $(n/N)^2$ is the chance that two picks both belong to it. Adding over all species gives the chance that two random individuals are the same species. Subtracting from 1 gives the chance they are different: a natural measure of diversity. If one species dominates, two picks are usually the same, and D is low.

blocks.title: Two meadows
blocks.q: Meadow A has 25 each of four plant species (100 plants). Meadow B has 85, 5, 5 and 5. Find D for each.
blocks.a: A: D = 0.75; B: D = 0.27. Same richness, but A is far more even, so far more diverse.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: Same four species, very different evenness.

blocks.title: Adding a species
blocks.q: A pond has 30 snails and 30 water beetles (D = 0.5). A third species, 30 water striders, moves in. What is D now?
steps: Each fraction is now 30/90 = 1/3.
blocks.a: About 0.67: more richness raised D.

blocks.html: In the field, ecologists count individuals in quadrats or along transects, then compute D for each site. Comparing D before and after a disturbance, or between a protected and an unprotected area, turns "it looks less diverse" into a number that can be tracked. Two cautions: D depends on how thoroughly a site was sampled, and it says nothing about which species are present, so a site full of invasive species can still score high.

Two slips: adding the fractions without squaring them (the plain fractions always add to 1, so D would always be 0), and forgetting to subtract from 1, which turns a low-diversity place into a high number. Check: one species only must give D = 0.

blocks.html: A diversity index says how many species a community has and how evenly; it does not say what holds the community together. You met keystone species before. Here we look at the forces that shape a community from above and from below.

items: Top-down control: predators limit herbivores, which lets plants thrive. Remove the predator, and the effect cascades down: a trophic cascade. Where sea otters were hunted out, sea urchins boomed and grazed kelp forests down to bare rock; where otters returned, kelp recovered.
Bottom-up control: nutrients limit producers, which limit everything that eats them. Add nutrients and producers grow.

Keystone species: a species with an effect far larger than its numbers. When the ecologist Robert Paine removed the sea star Pisaster from tide pools, mussels took over and many other species disappeared.
Ecosystem engineers: species that build or change habitat, such as beavers, whose dams turn streams into ponds and wetlands.
Invasive species: species introduced to a new place where they spread and harm the community, often because their natural predators and diseases are missing.

blocks.name: bi-foodweb
blocks.cap: Remove a species from the pond web and see the first effects on its food and its predators.

blocks.html: Communities are shaped from the top down (predators) and the bottom up (nutrients). Keystone species, ecosystem engineers and invasive species can restructure them. More nutrients do not always mean a healthier community.

Why can adding nutrients hurt a lake? Nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizer runoff or sewage feed a bloom of algae. The algae soon die, and bacteria decomposing them use up the dissolved oxygen through respiration. Fish and other animals suffocate. This process is called eutrophication. The bottom of the food web grew; the community collapsed.

blocks.title: A trophic cascade
blocks.q: In a kelp forest, otters eat urchins and urchins eat kelp. Predict what happens to urchins and kelp if otters disappear.
steps: Otters gone: urchins are no longer eaten, so urchins increase.
More urchins graze more kelp, so kelp decreases.
blocks.a: Urchins up, kelp down: a cascade two levels below the predator.

blocks.name: bi-chart

opts.xlabel: Weeks after a large input of fertilizer runoff

blocks.cap: Eutrophication in a lake (illustrative): algae bloom, then crash, and oxygen falls as they decompose.

blocks.title: Reading the lake data
blocks.q: In the graph, why does oxygen rise first and then fall far below where it started?
steps: Weeks 2 to 4: the algae bloom, and their photosynthesis adds oxygen.
After week 4: the algae die, and decomposers respire as they break them down.
Respiration uses more oxygen than the shrinking algae can make.
blocks.a: The bloom first adds oxygen; its decomposition then uses it up.

blocks.html: Thinking that adding nutrients always makes a community healthier. Extra nitrogen and phosphorus can cause algal blooms that use up the oxygen. And remember that effects spread through the web: removing one species changes its prey, its predators and, through them, species it never touched.

blocks.html: Communities change all the time, but some disruptions are fast and large: an invasive species arrives, a habitat is cleared, a pollutant spreads, a disease sweeps through, or the climate shifts. Community structure tells us how effects spread through a web. Population genetics tells us which populations can adapt.

items: Invasive species: brought to a place outside their range, they can outcompete or eat native species. Zebra mussels, for example, spread through North American lakes and rivers after arriving from Eurasia.
Habitat loss and fragmentation: clearing land and splitting habitats into small patches shrinks and isolates populations.
Pollution: excess nutrients cause algal blooms; some chemicals build up in food chains.
Disease: a fungal blight from Asia, first recorded in New York in 1904, killed roughly four billion American chestnut trees in the first half of the 1900s.
Changes in climate: warmer seas can make corals expel the algae that live in them (coral bleaching), and shifting temperatures change where species can live.

blocks.html: Disruptions can change populations fast. They do not hit every species equally: species with narrow niches, small ranges or little genetic variation are most vulnerable. A population with more variation is more likely to include individuals that can survive a change, so it can adapt by natural selection.

blocks.name: bi-selection
blocks.cap: A population with varied colors meets a new background. Run some generations: variation is what selection works on.

blocks.html: Natural selection can only choose among the variants a population already has. If every individual is nearly identical, as in a field of one crop variety grown from cuttings, a new disease that kills one kills them all. In a varied population, a few individuals may happen to resist it. They survive and leave offspring, and the population recovers with the resistance now common. That is why genetic variation is called the raw material of adaptation, and why bottlenecks (Genetic Drift) leave populations at risk.

blocks.title: Who is hit hardest?
blocks.q: A warm spell damages a mountain meadow. Which is most at risk: a plant found only on that mountain's cool peak, a widespread grass, or a weed that grows almost anywhere?
steps: The peak plant has a narrow niche and nowhere cooler to move.
The grass and the weed are generalists with wide ranges.
blocks.a: The plant found only on the peak. Some generalists may even gain from the change.

blocks.title: Variation and survival
blocks.q: In a population of 2,000 snails, 3% carry an allele that protects them from a new parasite. The parasite kills 95% of unprotected snails and none of the protected ones. How many snails survive, and what share of the survivors carry the allele?
steps: Protected: 3% of 2,000 = 60; all survive.
Unprotected: 1,940; 5% survive = 97.
Survivors: 60 + 97 = 157; protected share: 60 / 157 ≈ 38%.
blocks.a: 157 survive, and about 38% of them carry the allele, up from 3%: selection in one generation.

blocks.html: Thinking a disruption affects every species equally. Species with narrow niches or little genetic variation are hit hardest, while some generalists may gain. Where people disagree about how to respond, for example how to balance land use and conservation, the science describes the effects; choosing among the trade-offs is a decision people weigh together.
